topics.title: Introduction, history and symptoms
topics.summary: CLB Lecture 1 (Dr Dutta, week 1): why people choose contact lenses, how contact lenses developed, what modern contact lens practice covers, and how to take a contact lens history and symptoms, spot contraindications and take the baseline measurements (HVID and pupil size).
keyPoints: Why contact lenses: more natural vision and a wider field (no frame), optics stay aligned with the eye, no fogging or rain on lenses, better for anisometropia and irregular astigmatism, good for sport and under goggles, cosmetic benefits, UV protection and myopia control.

Contact lens practice now covers optical correction, myopia control, therapeutic/medical lenses (after disease, surgery or trauma), aesthetic lenses and specialist uses (e.g. drug delivery, scleral lenses).

Lens types: spherical or toric, single vision or multifocal; rigid gas permeable (corneal or scleral); soft (hydrogel or silicone hydrogel); daily disposable, planned replacement or reusable; plus ortho-K. Silicone hydrogel wear is increasing.

History structure: patient preferences (why CLs, current lens/brand/modality, years of wear, hours per day, solution, quality-of-life benefits), lifestyle (age, recreation, occupation and hobbies, environment, digital devices), health (general and ocular health, surgery, medication, family history, allergies) and refractive state (spherical, astigmatic, presbyopic, paediatric/myopia).

Symptoms: use SOCRATES — site (one or both eyes), onset, character (glare, blur; burning, gritty, itchy, watery, tired), timing, exacerbating/relieving factors (near/distance, with lenses) and severity.
Medication matters: some systemic drugs reduce tear volume or blink rate, or change corneal sensitivity; topical drops and their preservatives can be absorbed by soft lenses.
Baseline measurements: HVID (range about 10–14 mm, average 11.7 mm), pupil size in room and dim light, and keratometry/topography.
examTraps: Forgetting to ask about medication — it can reduce blinking and tear volume and cause lens intolerance.
Measuring pupil size only in room light — dim-light size matters for presbyopic and myopia-control designs.
Skipping pre-fitting counselling (risks, costs and what to do in an emergency) and not documenting it.

diagram.description: Timeline of contact lens history: early ideas (Celsus, Da Vinci, Descartes 1637, de la Hire 1685), Thomas Young 1801, John Herschel 1827, then Fick, Kalt and Müller in the late 1880s, and Zeiss lathe-cut lenses.

goDeeper.heading: A short history of contact lenses
goDeeper.body: Early ideas don't really describe contact lenses: Celsus used linen discs after pterygium surgery; a Leonardo da Vinci manuscript was long thought to show the 'invention' of contact lenses (later disproved); Descartes described a water-filled tube (1637) and de la Hire a fluid that might correct myopia (1685). Thomas Young (1801) and Sir John Herschel (1827) deserve more credit — Herschel suggested that for badly irregular corneas a transparent jelly in a glass capsule, or a mould of the cornea, could give clear vision. In the 1880s Adolf Fick made moulded lenses (from rabbit and cadaver eyes) and tried them on himself, Eugène Kalt noticed lenses could change corneal shape, and August Müller, a −14.00 D medical student, corrected his own myopia with glass lenses he could wear for about 30 minutes. Zeiss later lathe-cut lenses, giving better optics and the first commercial trial lenses.

goDeeper.heading: Conditions and contraindications
goDeeper.body: Ask about allergy and hay fever (atopy), diabetes, systemic inflammatory disease such as sarcoidosis (uveitis), thyroid eye disease, skin conditions linked to blepharitis (seborrhoeic dermatitis, atopic eczema, acne rosacea) and previous eye surgery — with onset, type, how well controlled, and family history. Possible contraindications include a very low refractive error, a need for horizontal prism, eye infection or inflammation, recurrent corneal erosion, diabetes, sinus and allergy problems, sensitive or dry eyes and poor blinking, acne rosacea or seborrhoeic conditions, and adverse (e.g. dusty) environments. Considering these first saves everyone time and money.

goDeeper.heading: Medication and contact lens wear
goDeeper.body: Systemic: antihistamines, antidepressants and diuretics can reduce tear production; tranquillisers, muscle relaxants and alcohol can reduce blink rate and amplitude; oestrogens and some pain relievers can change corneal sensitivity; blood pressure drugs and anticholinergics can affect vision; some drugs affecting fluid balance can cause corneal oedema. Topical: soft lenses (especially hydrogels) can absorb and retain drops and their preservatives, which can cause irritation or toxicity. Review medications at every visit.

goDeeper.heading: Before fitting: counselling
goDeeper.body: Discuss and document: the recommended lens type, modality of wear, care and cleaning regimen, possible risks and complications, how long until full-time wear, possible visual compromise or discomfort, what to do in an emergency, and the costs involved.

goDeeper.heading: Baseline measurements
goDeeper.body: HVID (horizontal visible iris diameter) can be measured with a topographer, autorefractor, slit lamp graticule, aberrometer or PD ruler — normal range about 10–14 mm, average 11.7 mm. Measure pupil diameter with a ruler (or Burton lamp) in room light (photopic, average) and dim light (scotopic, maximum) — important for presbyopic and myopia-control lenses. Add K readings or topography, and corneal shape/scleral dimensions if needed. Vertical palpebral aperture is rarely used nowadays.

mcq.q: What is the average horizontal visible iris diameter (HVID)?

options.feedback: Yes — with a range of roughly 10–14 mm.
That's closer to a typical soft lens base curve.
That's a typical soft lens total diameter, not HVID.
That's more like a pupil diameter.

mcq.explanation: HVID helps choose lens diameter; average 11.7 mm, range about 10–14 mm.

mcq.q: A prospective wearer takes antihistamines most of the year. Why does this matter?

options.text: They can reduce tears, causing dryness and intolerance
options.feedback: Right — ask about it and consider the lens and care choice.

options.text: They change the lens power the patient needs
options.feedback: They don't change the refractive correction.

options.text: They make the lenses fit more tightly on the eye
It doesn't matter for contact lens wearers
options.feedback: Systemic medication can affect tears and comfort.

mcq.explanation: Systemic drugs such as antihistamines, antidepressants and diuretics can reduce tear volume.

mcq.q: Which is listed as a possible contraindication to contact lens wear?

options.feedback: Yes — along with active infection or inflammation.
Moderate myopia is a common reason to fit CLs.
Sport is a reason to choose CLs.
CLs are often better than spectacles for anisometropia.

mcq.explanation: Contraindications include low refractive error, horizontal prism, infection/inflammation, recurrent erosions, dry eyes and poor blinking, and adverse environments.

mcq.q: Which is an optical advantage of contact lenses over spectacles?

options.text: They move with the eye: no prism in eccentric gaze
They always cost less than spectacles
They never need replacing once fitted

mcq.explanation: Contact lenses move with the eye, so you look through the optical centre in every direction of gaze. There's no prism or peripheral aberration as with spectacles.

mcq.q: Why measure HVID before fitting?

options.text: It guides the total lens diameter
It sets the lens power needed
It isn't needed for any fitting

mcq.explanation: HVID (horizontal visible iris diameter) estimates corneal diameter, which guides the total lens diameter for good coverage.

mcq.q: A wearer reports gritty, tired eyes late in the day. Which framework helps explore the symptom?

options.feedback: Yes: site, onset, character, timing and so on.

mcq.explanation: SOCRATES (site, onset, character, radiation, associations, timing, exacerbating or relieving factors, severity) structures questions about a symptom.

mcq.q: Why ask about systemic medication at a contact lens appointment?

options.text: Some drugs reduce tears, blinking or corneal sensation
To choose the right lens colour
It's only needed for spectacle wearers
To work out the lens material's Dk

mcq.explanation: Drugs such as antihistamines, antidepressants, isotretinoin and beta-blockers can reduce tear production, blinking or corneal sensation, which affects lens tolerance and safety.

mcq.q: Which is a therapeutic use of contact lenses?

options.text: A bandage lens after disease, surgery or trauma
Changing the colour of the eyes

mcq.explanation: Therapeutic (bandage) lenses protect and promote healing of the cornea after disease, surgery or trauma, and relieve pain.

mcq.q: Which pupil sizes should be measured at baseline?

options.text: In room light and dim light

options.feedback: It's used for optic zone choice.

mcq.explanation: Pupil size in room light and in dim light guides optic zone and multifocal design choices, and helps explain haloes at night.

mcq.q: Who made one of the first glass scleral contact lenses, in 1888?

options.feedback: Yes; Kalt and Müller worked on lenses at about the same time.

mcq.explanation: In 1888 Adolf Fick made one of the first glass scleral lenses. Kalt and Müller worked on similar lenses at about the same time.

mcq.q: Who developed the first soft hydrogel (HEMA) lenses?
mcq.explanation: Otto Wichterle and Drahoslav Lím developed HEMA hydrogel soft lenses in Czechoslovakia in the late 1950s and 1960s.

mcq.q: Which material made the first corneal hard lenses possible?
mcq.explanation: PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate) made the first corneal hard lenses possible, introduced by Tuohy in 1948.

mcq.q: Which is a cosmetic reason people choose contact lenses?

options.text: Not wanting to be seen in spectacles

mcq.explanation: Cosmetic reasons include not wanting to be seen wearing spectacles, or preferring how they look without them.

mcq.q: Which condition may be helped by a therapeutic bandage lens?
mcq.explanation: Bandage soft lenses protect the healing epithelium in recurrent corneal erosion and reduce pain.

mcq.q: Which is a contraindication to fitting lenses today?
mcq.explanation: Active anterior eye infection or inflammation is a contraindication. Lenses shouldn't be fitted until it has resolved.

mcq.q: Why ask about the patient's reasons for wanting lenses?

options.text: Motivation and lifestyle guide the lens choice
So you have a reason to refuse them
It isn't relevant to the fitting

mcq.explanation: Knowing why the patient wants lenses and how they will use them guides the choice of lens type and modality, and the expectations you set.

mcq.q: Why record baseline corneal staining and redness before fitting?

options.text: So lens-related changes can be spotted later
To help choose the lens colour

mcq.explanation: Baseline findings let you tell whether redness or staining at aftercare is new and lens-related.

mcq.q: Which occupation may make contact lens wear difficult?
mcq.explanation: Dusty, smoky or chemical environments can get under lenses and cause irritation, deposits or injury.

mcq.q: Which hobby is a strong reason to consider contact lenses?
mcq.explanation: Contact lenses suit contact sports because there's no frame to break or injure the eye, and they give a wide field of view.

mcq.q: Who sketched the idea of neutralising the cornea with water around 1508?

options.feedback: Yes, though it wasn't a lens.

mcq.explanation: Around 1508 Leonardo da Vinci sketched neutralising the cornea by looking through water. It wasn't a lens, but the principle is the same.

mcq.q: Who described a water-filled tube placed against the eye in 1636?
mcq.explanation: In 1636 René Descartes described a water-filled tube placed against the eye to change its optics.

mcq.q: Who made the first PMMA corneal lens, in 1948?
mcq.explanation: In 1948 Kevin Tuohy made the first PMMA corneal lens, much smaller than earlier sclerals.

mcq.q: When did the first silicone hydrogel lenses reach the market?
mcq.explanation: Silicone hydrogel lenses reached the market around 1998–1999, greatly raising oxygen supply.

mcq.q: When did daily disposable soft lenses appear?
mcq.explanation: Daily disposable soft lenses appeared in the mid-1990s.

mcq.q: In the UK, can cosmetic plano contact lenses be sold without supervision?

options.text: No: all lenses need registered supervision
Yes, they can be sold freely anywhere
Only around Halloween, as a costume item

mcq.explanation: Under UK law, all contact lenses, including cosmetic plano lenses, must be sold under the supervision of a registered practitioner.

mcq.q: To buy lenses online in the UK, a patient needs
mcq.explanation: UK suppliers must check a valid, in-date contact lens specification before supplying lenses, including online.

mcq.q: What does a contact lens specification include?

options.text: Lens type, parameters and expiry date
Only the power of each lens
Only the brand of lens worn

mcq.explanation: A specification must identify the lens fully: lens type or brand, its parameters (BOZR, TD, power) and the expiry date.

mcq.q: Which measurement helps choose a rigid lens size?
mcq.explanation: HVID and palpebral aperture help choose rigid lens diameter and predict whether it will sit between the lids or attach to the upper lid.

mcq.q: A typical palpebral aperture height is about
mcq.explanation: Typical palpebral aperture height is about 10 mm (roughly 8–11 mm).

mcq.q: Why assess lid tension before fitting?

options.text: It affects lens position and movement
To help choose the lens colour

mcq.explanation: Lid tension and position affect how a lens sits, moves and centres, especially for rigid lenses.

mcq.q: Why check blink rate and completeness?

options.text: To help choose the lens colour

mcq.explanation: Incomplete or infrequent blinking reduces tear exchange and spreading, causing drying, staining and deposits.

mcq.q: Which is a relative contraindication to lens wear?
mcq.explanation: Poorly controlled diabetes reduces corneal sensitivity and healing, and raises infection risk, so lens wear needs extra care.

mcq.q: Which therapeutic use is common after PRK laser surgery?
mcq.explanation: After PRK, a bandage soft lens protects the healing epithelium and reduces pain.

mcq.q: Which condition commonly uses rigid lenses for vision?
mcq.explanation: In keratoconus, rigid lenses (corneal or scleral) give a smooth optical surface that masks irregular astigmatism.

mcq.q: Which patient group has a clear optical benefit from contact lenses?
mcq.explanation: Contact lenses reduce the difference in image size between the eyes (aniseikonia) in high anisometropia.

mcq.q: How do you check if a soft lens is inside out?

options.text: The 'taco' test or checking the edge shape
Put it in the eye and wait a day

mcq.explanation: In the taco test, gently fold the lens: the edges should point straight up. Viewed from the side, a correct lens has a bowl shape, while an inside-out one has flared edges.

mcq.q: Why teach insertion and removal before the patient leaves?
mcq.explanation: Patients must be able to insert and remove lenses safely and hygienically before leaving, or they may have problems at home.

mcq.q: A patient with poor dexterity may struggle with
mcq.explanation: Arthritis, tremor or poor dexterity can make inserting, removing and cleaning lenses hard.

mcq.q: Which history question is most important for contact lens safety?

options.text: Water exposure and sleeping in lenses

mcq.explanation: Sleeping in lenses and water exposure are the biggest modifiable risks for serious infection, so ask about both.

mcq.q: Why might a patient with severe dry eye be a poor candidate?

options.text: They have a high eye pressure

mcq.explanation: Lenses split and thin the tear film, so a patient with severe dry eye may get more dryness, discomfort and complications.

mcq.q: Can children wear contact lenses?

options.text: Yes, if they can handle them hygienically
Never: lenses are for adults only
Only rigid lenses, never soft ones

mcq.explanation: Children can wear contact lenses if they (with their parents) can handle them hygienically and responsibly. There's no minimum legal age.

mcq.q: Which slit lamp findings should be recorded at baseline?
mcq.explanation: Record baseline redness, staining, lids, tear film and limbal vessels, so lens-related changes can be spotted at aftercare.

mcq.q: Myopia control contact lenses are used for
mcq.explanation: Myopia control lenses (e.g. dual-focus soft or ortho-k) are used to slow myopia progression in children.

mcq.q: Which is a disadvantage of contact lenses?

options.text: No frame to get in the way

mcq.explanation: Disadvantages include the risk of infection and complications, and the ongoing cost of lenses and solutions.

mcq.q: When was the first disposable soft lens launched (frequent replacement era)?
mcq.explanation: Disposable and frequent-replacement soft lenses were launched in the late 1980s.

mcq.q: Prosthetic contact lenses are used to

options.text: improve the look of a disfigured eye

mcq.explanation: Prosthetic lenses (with painted or opaque irises and pupils) improve the appearance of a scarred or disfigured eye.

mcq.q: Who can legally fit contact lenses in the UK?
mcq.explanation: In the UK, contact lenses can be fitted only by registered optometrists, contact lens opticians or registered medical practitioners.

mcq.q: Why is aftercare important?
mcq.explanation: Aftercare checks fit, ocular health and compliance, so complications are caught early.

mcq.q: Which history detail suggests poor candidacy?
mcq.explanation: Poor hygiene or not following instructions are major risk factors for complications, so these patients may be poor candidates.

cases.scenario: A 51-year-old wants contact lenses for tennis. She has hay fever and takes antihistamines in summer, works long days on a laptop, and wears varifocals (add +1.50).
cases.question: What would you focus on in her history and before fitting?
cases.modelAnswer: Explore her reasons and wearing times (sport), atopy and antihistamine use (dryness, possible daily disposables in hay fever season), screen use and symptoms (SOCRATES), general and eye health. She's presbyopic, so discuss multifocal CLs or monovision and measure pupil size in room and dim light; take HVID and K readings. Counsel on lens type, wear, care, risks, costs and emergencies, and document it.

topics.title: Keratometry
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 3 lecture: the keratometer measures the radius of the central cornea (really the tear film acting as a convex mirror) in its two principal meridians. Know how it works, what it assumes, where errors come from and what you use it for.
keyPoints: The cornea gives about two thirds of the eye's power (about 43 D). Radii range from about 7.4 to 8.8 mm; record e.g. 7.90 @ 150; 7.85 @ 60.
Principle: an object of known size at a fixed distance is imaged by the cornea as a convex mirror; radius ≈ 2 × working distance × image height ÷ mire separation.

Working distance is checked with a Scheiner disc (doubled image unless aligned); eye movement is overcome by doubling the image with a prism. Fixed doubling (Bausch & Lomb, one position) or variable doubling (Javal-Schiotz, two positions).
Assumptions: a spherical arc, principal meridians at 90°, an on-axis measure, and a back surface with −10% of the front power, hence n = 1.3375 (USA: D = 0.3375 ÷ r).
Errors: operator (focusing, proximal accommodation, alignment, orientation) and patient (corneal distortion, unsteady fixation). Distorted mires suggest an irregular cornea.
Uses: baseline data, corneal astigmatism (0.05 mm difference ≈ 0.25 D), choosing a first lens and whether RGP or toric is needed, RGP flexure, post-wear oedema or moulding, and verifying lens radius.
In clinic: take three readings of each meridian in each eye and average them.
examTraps: Forgetting it only samples a small central area (about 3 mm): topography maps the rest.
Mixing up meridian and axis when recording.
Assuming refractive astigmatism equals corneal astigmatism: lenticular astigmatism can differ.

diagram.description: Two corneal topography maps side by side. Left: regular with-the-rule astigmatism — a symmetrical vertical 'bow tie' of warmer (steeper) colours. Right: keratoconus — an asymmetric patch of hot colours inferiorly. Colour scale bar: red/orange = steep, blue = flat.
labels: Colour scale: red = steep, blue = flat

goDeeper.heading: Test-your-knowledge answers
goDeeper.body: Keratometry readings represent corneal curvature, in millimetres or dioptres. A hyperbola has e² over 1. Against-the-rule astigmatism gives a horizontal bow tie on a topography map.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: HVID and pupil size
goDeeper.body: Horizontal visible iris diameter (about 11.5–12 mm) and pupil size are measured alongside K readings to choose total diameter and optic zone; the week 5 rigid lens lecture gives the rules (TD about 2 mm less than HVID; BOZD about 1 mm larger than the pupil).

flashcards.back: About 45.00 D.
Vertical meridian steeper than horizontal.
Asymmetric inferior steepening (hot colours inferiorly).
Bausch & Lomb: fixed doubling, both meridians measured from one position. Javal-Schiotz: variable doubling, two positions.
Focusing, proximal accommodation, alignment and orientation of the instrument.

mcq.q: K readings are 7.90 @ 180 and 7.60 @ 90. What is the corneal astigmatism, approximately?

options.feedback: Yes: 337.5/7.90 ≈ 42.72 D, 337.5/7.60 ≈ 44.41 D; difference ≈ 1.70 D, vertical steeper.
The vertical meridian (90) has the smaller radius, so it's steeper — with-the-rule.
0.30 is the difference in mm, not dioptres.
Convert each radius to dioptres and subtract.

mcq.explanation: Convert each K to dioptres with 337.5/r and subtract. The steeper (smaller radius) meridian tells you the type.

mcq.q: Refractive astigmatism is −2.00 × 180; corneal astigmatism is 2.00 D with-the-rule. With a spherical RGP, what residual astigmatism would you expect?

options.feedback: Right — the astigmatism is corneal, which the tear lens corrects.
That would be the case if it were all lenticular.
They don't add; the tear lens cancels corneal astigmatism.
Comparing refractive and corneal astigmatism lets you estimate it.

mcq.explanation: Residual astigmatism ≈ refractive astigmatism − corneal astigmatism (in matching form). Equal amounts at matching axes leave little residual.

mcq.q: What do keratometry readings represent?

options.feedback: Yes: the radius of curvature of the central cornea in each principal meridian.
Horizontal visible iris diameter is measured separately.

mcq.explanation: The radius of curvature of the central cornea in each principal meridian.

mcq.q: A keratometer reads 7.50 mm. What is that in dioptres (n = 1.3375)?
mcq.explanation: K readings can be given in millimetres or dioptres; dioptres ≈ 337.5 ÷ radius in mm.

original.q: Which units are typically used in keratometry?

options.feedback: Yes: radius in mm, or power in D from F = (n − 1)/r.
Degrees give the meridian, not the reading itself.
Degrees give the meridian, not the reading itself.
Those belong to pachymetry and tonometry.

original.explanation: Test-your-knowledge question 2. The lecture writes readings as e.g. 7.90 @ 150 and notes the USA uses dioptres.

mcq.q: Convert a corneal radius of 7.50 mm to power (n = 1.3375).
How does a keratometer overcome constant small eye movements?

options.text: It doubles the image with a prism

mcq.explanation: Constant eye movements would make the mire image impossible to measure, so a prism doubles it. The two images move together, and their separation (which sets the image size) can still be read steadily.

mcq.q: What does a Scheiner disc in a keratometer check?

options.feedback: Yes: the image doubles unless it's aligned.

mcq.explanation: The Scheiner disc makes the mire image double when the instrument is out of focus, so you know the working distance is correct before you read.

mcq.q: Why is n = 1.3375 used instead of 1.376?

options.text: It allows for the back surface, giving total power
It's the refractive index of the tears
It's the refractive index of the lens

mcq.explanation: Keratometers measure only the front surface. The fictitious index 1.3375 lowers the result to allow for the negative back surface, giving an estimate of total corneal power.

mcq.q: A difference of 0.05 mm between principal meridians is roughly how much corneal astigmatism?
mcq.explanation: Near 7.8 mm, each 0.05 mm of radius is about 0.25 D (337.5 ÷ 7.8² × 0.05 ≈ 0.28 D), so 0.05 mm between meridians is about 0.25 D of corneal astigmatism.

mcq.q: How many readings of each meridian are taken in clinic?

options.feedback: Not enough for a reliable reading.

mcq.explanation: Taking three readings per meridian and averaging them reduces measurement error and gives a more repeatable K value.

mcq.q: What's the power of a corneal radius of 8.00 mm (n = 1.3375)?
A cornea measures 45.00 D. What's its radius?
In with-the-rule corneal astigmatism, which meridian is steeper?
mcq.explanation: With-the-rule corneal astigmatism has the vertical meridian steeper (more powerful) than the horizontal. It is common in young eyes.

mcq.q: About what central area does a keratometer measure?
mcq.explanation: The keratometer's mires reflect from two points on a ring roughly 3 mm across, so it only samples the central cornea, not the whole surface.

mcq.q: A one-position keratometer

options.text: measures only one meridian at a time

mcq.explanation: A one-position keratometer (e.g. Bausch & Lomb) has separate doubling for both principal meridians, so both are measured without rotating it through 90°.

mcq.q: Distorted keratometer mires suggest
mcq.explanation: Regular mires need a smooth, regular reflecting surface. Distorted mires point to irregular astigmatism (e.g. keratoconus, scarring) or a poor tear film.

mcq.q: Which surface does a keratometer use as a convex mirror?
mcq.explanation: The front surface of the cornea (with its tear film) acts as a convex mirror. The size of the reflected mire image gives the radius of curvature.

mcq.q: How is a keratometer calibrated?

options.text: With steel balls of known radius
With a ruler against the mires
With a trial lens in the holder

mcq.explanation: Steel balls of precisely known radius are measured as a check. Any error is used to correct or recalibrate the instrument.

mcq.q: Refractive −0.50 × 180, corneal 1.50 D with-the-rule. Residual astigmatism?
mcq.explanation: Residual = refractive − corneal. Corneal 1.50 D WTR is −1.50 × 180, so −0.50 × 180 − (−1.50 × 180) = +1.00 × 180, which is −1.00 × 90 in minus cylinder.

mcq.q: Why does residual astigmatism matter for rigid lenses?

options.text: A spherical rigid lens won't correct it
It makes rigid lenses fit tighter
It doesn't matter for rigid lenses

mcq.explanation: A spherical rigid lens's tear lens neutralises corneal astigmatism only. Residual (mainly lenticular) astigmatism stays uncorrected and may need a toric design.

mcq.q: What is the power of a 7.70 mm radius (n = 1.3375)?
What is the power of a 7.40 mm radius?
A cornea measures 42.00 D. What's its radius?
K readings 7.80 @ 180 and 7.50 @ 90. Corneal astigmatism?
mcq.explanation: 7.80 mm ≈ 43.27 D (horizontal) and 7.50 mm = 45.00 D (vertical). The vertical is steeper by about 1.75 D, which is with-the-rule.

mcq.q: K readings are 7.60 @ 180 and 7.85 @ 90. What kind of corneal astigmatism is this?

options.feedback: Yes: the horizontal meridian is steeper.

mcq.explanation: Against-the-rule: horizontal meridian steeper. With-the-rule: vertical steeper.

original.q: In against-the-rule corneal astigmatism, which meridian is steeper?

mcq.q: Javal's rule estimates
mcq.explanation: Javal's rule predicts total (refractive) astigmatism from corneal astigmatism, roughly 1.25 × corneal plus 0.50 D against-the-rule (−0.50 × 90).

mcq.q: A typical average central corneal radius is about
mcq.explanation: The average central corneal radius is about 7.8 mm, which equals about 43 D with n = 1.3375.

mcq.q: K readings over about 48 D may suggest
mcq.explanation: K readings over about 48 D (radius under about 7.0 mm) are unusually steep and raise suspicion of keratoconus, especially with irregular mires or high astigmatism.

mcq.q: The Javal-Schiøtz keratometer is a
mcq.explanation: The Javal-Schiøtz keratometer measures one meridian at a time and must be rotated 90° to measure the other, so it is a two-position instrument.

mcq.q: The Bausch & Lomb keratometer
mcq.explanation: The Bausch & Lomb keratometer is a one-position instrument with separate horizontal and vertical doubling, so both meridians are read without rotating.

mcq.q: Before taking readings, you should
mcq.explanation: Focusing the eyepiece for your own eye first stops your refractive error or accommodation from causing measurement errors.

mcq.q: How are K readings usually recorded?
mcq.explanation: Ks are recorded as radius (mm) or power (D) for each principal meridian with its axis, e.g. 7.80 @ 180 / 7.60 @ 90.

mcq.q: The mean K is

options.text: the steeper of the two Ks
the flatter of the two Ks

mcq.explanation: Mean K is the average of the two principal meridian readings. It is used in IOL calculations and some contact lens fitting.

mcq.q: Keratometry is needed for IOL power calculation together with
mcq.explanation: IOL power formulas need corneal power (K) and axial length to predict the lens power that gives the target refraction.

mcq.q: Keratometer accuracy is roughly
mcq.explanation: A well-used keratometer gives readings to about ±0.02 mm (around ±0.12 D) on a regular cornea.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a use of keratometry?
mcq.explanation: Keratometry measures corneal curvature. Intraocular pressure is measured by tonometry.

mcq.q: The flattest K is important in rigid lens fitting because

options.text: the BOZR is chosen from it

mcq.explanation: Rigid lens BOZR is usually chosen relative to flat K (on K or slightly flatter) to get an alignment fit.

mcq.q: Residual astigmatism is usually mostly
mcq.explanation: Residual astigmatism is the part not accounted for by the front cornea. It mostly comes from the crystalline lens, with a small contribution from the back cornea.

mcq.q: A keratometer cannot measure
mcq.explanation: The keratometer only samples a central ring about 3 mm across, so the peripheral cornea needs topography instead.

mcq.q: Which instrument maps the whole cornea?
mcq.explanation: A corneal topographer (videokeratoscope or Scheimpflug system) maps curvature across the whole cornea, while a keratometer only measures the centre.

mcq.q: What does pachymetry measure?
mcq.explanation: Pachymetry measures corneal thickness, by ultrasound or optically. It matters for glaucoma (thin corneas read low on IOP), keratoconus and refractive surgery.

mcq.q: Refractive −1.50 × 180 and corneal 1.50 D WTR. Residual astigmatism?

options.feedback: Yes: the cornea accounts for it all.

mcq.explanation: Corneal 1.50 D WTR is −1.50 × 180, which equals the refractive cylinder, so residual = −1.50 × 180 − (−1.50 × 180) ≈ zero.

mcq.q: Refractive −0.50 × 90 and corneal 1.00 D WTR. Residual astigmatism?
mcq.explanation: Residual = refractive − corneal. Corneal 1.00 D WTR is −1.00 × 180, which equals +1.00 × 90, so −0.50 × 90 − (+1.00 × 90) = −1.50 × 90.

mcq.q: Why record which meridian each K belongs to?
mcq.explanation: Knowing which meridian is steep gives the axis and type (with-, against-the-rule or oblique) of corneal astigmatism, which you need for fitting and comparison.

mcq.q: K readings that change between visits may suggest
mcq.explanation: Ks that change between visits suggest progressive ectasia (e.g. keratoconus) or contact lens-induced corneal warpage, so investigate further, for example with topography.

mcq.q: Mire doubling in keratometers is used to
mcq.explanation: Doubling lets the image size be measured by aligning two moving images against each other, so eye movements don't spoil the reading.

mcq.q: After rigid lens wear, K readings may
mcq.explanation: Rigid (especially PMMA or poorly fitting) lenses can mould the cornea. This corneal warpage changes Ks for a while after the lenses are removed.

mcq.q: A 0.10 mm difference in radius near 7.8 mm is about
mcq.explanation: Near 7.8 mm, 0.05 mm is about 0.25–0.28 D, so 0.10 mm is about 0.50–0.60 D.

mcq.q: What are the 'principal meridians'?
mcq.explanation: The principal meridians are the steepest and flattest meridians of an astigmatic cornea. In regular astigmatism they are 90° apart.

mcq.q: Oblique corneal astigmatism has its principal meridians

options.text: at the same angle as each other

mcq.explanation: Oblique astigmatism has its principal meridians between 30° and 60° or between 120° and 150°, i.e. away from the horizontal and vertical.

cases.scenario: Keratometry on a new contact lens patient gives 7.80 mm along 180 and 7.60 mm along 90.
cases.question: How much corneal astigmatism is this, of what type, and how does it guide lens choice?
cases.modelAnswer: A difference of 0.20 mm is about 1.00 D of corneal astigmatism, using the rule that 0.05 mm is roughly 0.25 D. The vertical meridian is steeper, so it is with-the-rule. Compare it with the spectacle cylinder: if they roughly match, the astigmatism is corneal and a spherical rigid lens would correct it through the tear lens, while a soft lens would need to be toric for about 0.75 DC or more. If they differ, there is lenticular astigmatism, which a spherical rigid lens will leave uncorrected.

topics.askClaude: Give me 5 sets of K readings, ask me to convert them to dioptres and name the type of corneal astigmatism, then check my answers.

topics.title: Soft lens materials: hydrogel and silicone hydrogel
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 9 and week 12 lectures: what an ideal soft lens material needs, how oxygen reaches the cornea and is measured (Dk, Dk/t, EOP), what hypoxia does, how wettability is tested, and how hydrogels and silicone hydrogels compare.
keyPoints: Ideal material: meets the cornea's oxygen needs, inert, wets well, resists spoilage, biocompatible and comfortable, dimensionally stable, durable, transparent, low-maintenance and easy to make.

Corneal oxygen comes from the air with eyes open, the palpebral conjunctiva with eyes closed, plus the limbus and aqueous. Air is 21% oxygen; under closed lids about 8%; the cornea swells 3–4% overnight anyway.
Dk (permeability) = diffusion × solubility, a material property quoted at 34°C (range 0–300 × 10⁻¹¹). Dk/t (transmissibility) depends on thickness (range 0–200 × 10⁻⁹).
The original Fatt method overestimates Dk (edge and boundary effects); corrected values are about 25% lower and coulometric values 5–10% lower again. EOP results depend heavily on method.
Holden-Mertz: Dk/t 24 (EOP 9.9%) for daily wear and 87 (EOP 17.9%) for extended wear; later estimates 35 and 125 (Harvitt and Bonanno) or 175 (Smith et al.).
Low Dk/t causes microcysts, oedema (striae), lower corneal pH, endothelial blebs and polymegethism, and neovascularisation.

Hydrogel Dk rises with water content but can't reach extended-wear needs. Silicone hydrogels separate oxygen (silicone) and water (hydrogel) pathways: first generation surface-treated, second internal wetting, third non-TRIS (e.g. comfilcon), then water-gradient designs.

Silicone hydrogels remove hypoxic complications; early generations had more mechanical events; mucin balls can occur; CIE and MK rates are unchanged when modality is matched. Hydrogels like etafilcon A still give a quiet eye in daily wear.
examTraps: Mixing up Dk (material) and Dk/t (lens).
Assuming more water means more oxygen in silicone hydrogels: that's only true for hydrogels.
Thinking silicone hydrogels lowered the rate of microbial keratitis: they didn't.

diagram.description: Graph with water content (%) on the x-axis and Dk on the y-axis. Hydrogel line rises gently with water content. Silicone hydrogel points sit much higher on the y-axis at lower water contents. Dashed horizontal lines mark daily-wear and overnight-wear oxygen thresholds (in Dk/t terms).
labels: Silicone hydrogel: high Dk, lower water

goDeeper.heading: Wettability tests
goDeeper.body: Sessile drop (water on the lens; under 90° is more wettable), Wilhelmy plate (advancing and receding angles as the lens is dipped) and captive bubble (air bubble under a lens in water, where advancing and receding angles are reversed). Poor wetting means worse vision, more deposits, discomfort and a home for microbes.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: thickness and modulus
goDeeper.body: Thicker lenses (high plus, toric ballast) have lower Dk/t, so check centre and peripheral thickness. Stiffer (higher modulus) silicone hydrogels can cause more mechanical problems such as SEALs and papillary conjunctivitis in some wearers.

flashcards.back: Dk = material permeability; Dk/t = transmissibility of a lens of thickness t.
About 24 × 10⁻⁹ Dk/t.
About 87 × 10⁻⁹ Dk/t.
Dk increases as water content increases.
Epithelial microcysts, stromal oedema (striae), endothelial blebs and polymegethism, neovascularisation.

flashcards.front: Oxygen at the cornea: open versus closed eye
flashcards.back: About 21% versus 8%.

mcq.q: Which change increases the Dk/t of a hydrogel lens of the same material?

options.feedback: Yes — Dk/t is inversely proportional to thickness.
Plus lenses get thicker centrally, lowering Dk/t.

mcq.explanation: Dk/t = Dk ÷ thickness, so for the same material a thinner lens transmits more oxygen.

mcq.q: A patient wants to sleep in lenses occasionally. Which material is more appropriate?

options.text: A silicone hydrogel approved for extended wear
options.feedback: Right — overnight wear needs much higher oxygen transmissibility.
Hydrogels can't reach overnight oxygen requirements.

options.text: Any lens if she removes it in the morning
options.feedback: Overnight wear risk depends on oxygen and lens approval.
This gives the least oxygen of all.

mcq.explanation: Closed-eye wear needs high Dk/t (Holden–Mertz ~87 × 10⁻⁹), which in practice means silicone hydrogels licensed for it — and it still carries more infection risk.

mcq.q: What does Dk/t describe?

options.text: Oxygen transmissibility of a particular lens

mcq.explanation: Dk is the material's oxygen permeability. Dk/t divides it by the lens thickness to give the transmissibility of that particular lens.

mcq.q: Why is Dk measured at 34°C?

options.text: Dk rises with heat; 34°C matches the eye
Lenses would melt above that temperature

mcq.explanation: Oxygen permeability rises with temperature, so Dk is quoted at about 34–35°C, the temperature of a lens on the eye.

mcq.q: What's the Holden-Mertz Dk/t to avoid swelling in extended wear?
mcq.explanation: Holden and Mertz found a Dk/t of about 24 avoids corneal swelling in daily wear and about 87 is needed to limit overnight swelling to normal levels in extended wear.

mcq.q: Why can a silicone hydrogel have a high Dk even with a low water content?

options.text: It has more water than a hydrogel

mcq.explanation: Silicone hydrogels have separate silicone (oxygen) and hydrogel (water) pathways.

original.q: How do silicone hydrogels give high Dk?

mcq.q: Which sign suggests chronic hypoxia?

options.feedback: Yes, also oedema, blebs, polymegethism and neovascularisation.

mcq.explanation: Epithelial microcysts are a classic sign of chronic hypoxia, alongside oedema, endothelial blebs, polymegethism and limbal neovascularisation.

mcq.q: In a sessile drop test, which contact angle means more wettable?

options.feedback: Yes: a flatter drop wets better.

mcq.explanation: A drop that spreads flat has a small contact angle. Angles below 90° mean the surface is more wettable.

mcq.q: How did the original Fatt Dk method compare with corrected values?
mcq.explanation: Fatt's original polarographic method didn't correct for edge and boundary effects, which overestimated Dk by about 25%.

mcq.q: What happened to microbial keratitis rates after silicone hydrogels arrived?
mcq.explanation: Silicone hydrogels greatly reduced hypoxic complications, but microbial keratitis rates in overnight wear didn't fall. The risk comes from more than hypoxia.

mcq.q: Two HEMA-based hydrogels are the same thickness; one is 38% water and one is 70%. Which transmits more oxygen?

options.feedback: Yes: hydrogel Dk rises with water content.

mcq.explanation: In conventional hydrogels oxygen travels through water, so Dk rises with water content.

original.q: In conventional hydrogels, how does Dk change with water content?

mcq.q: In silicone hydrogels, oxygen mostly passes through
mcq.explanation: Silicone is very permeable to oxygen, so in silicone hydrogels oxygen travels mainly through the silicone phase rather than the water.

mcq.q: A patient refitted into a stiff silicone hydrogel develops superior arcuate staining. Which property is most likely to blame?
mcq.explanation: The higher modulus of some silicone hydrogels is linked with SEALs and papillary conjunctivitis.

original.q: Silicone hydrogels' higher modulus can cause

mcq.q: In the FDA groups, which is high-water ionic?
mcq.explanation: FDA groups: I is low-water non-ionic, II is high-water non-ionic, III is low-water ionic, and IV is high-water ionic.

mcq.q: Group IV materials tend to attract
mcq.explanation: Group IV materials are high water and negatively charged, so they attract positively charged tear proteins, especially lysozyme.

mcq.q: Water content is the

options.text: share of the lens weight that's water
volume of tears under the lens
rate at which the lens dries out
amount of oxygen in the lens

mcq.explanation: Water content is the percentage of a fully hydrated lens's weight that is water.

mcq.q: The Holden-Mertz Dk/t needed to avoid swelling in daily wear is
mcq.explanation: Holden and Mertz's criterion for avoiding corneal swelling in daily (open-eye) wear is a Dk/t of about 24.

mcq.q: What's the unit of Dk?
mcq.explanation: Dk is expressed in barrer, quoted as × 10⁻¹¹ (cm²/s)(ml O₂/ml × mmHg).

mcq.q: Why are some silicone hydrogels plasma treated?
mcq.explanation: Silicone is hydrophobic, so many silicone hydrogels are plasma treated (or contain wetting agents) to make the surface wettable and resist lipid deposits.

mcq.q: High-water lenses in a dry office tend to
mcq.explanation: High-water lenses lose water in low humidity. Dehydration steepens and shrinks the lens, tightening the fit and causing dryness symptoms.

mcq.q: Hydrogel lenses are based on
mcq.explanation: Conventional hydrogels are made from hydrophilic polymers such as HEMA (hydroxyethyl methacrylate), which absorb water and become soft.

mcq.q: Why are ionic materials prone to lysozyme deposits?
mcq.explanation: Ionic materials carry a negative surface charge, which attracts the positively charged tear enzyme lysozyme.

mcq.q: Silicone hydrogels tend to attract more
mcq.explanation: The hydrophobic silicone in silicone hydrogels attracts more lipid deposits, while ionic hydrogels attract more protein.

mcq.q: 'Jelly bumps' on soft lenses are
mcq.explanation: 'Jelly bumps' are raised mixed deposits of calcium, lipid and protein on the lens surface.

mcq.q: An internal wetting agent in some silicone hydrogels is
mcq.explanation: PVP (polyvinylpyrrolidone) is built into some silicone hydrogels as an internal wetting agent to improve surface wettability.

mcq.q: Typical HEMA hydrogel Dk is about
mcq.explanation: HEMA-based hydrogels have a low Dk of about 8–10, because oxygen only passes through their water.

mcq.q: Typical silicone hydrogel Dk is about
mcq.explanation: Silicone hydrogels typically have a Dk of about 60–160 or more, many times that of conventional hydrogels.

mcq.q: A lens with Dk 100 and centre thickness 0.1 mm has Dk/t of about
mcq.explanation: Dk/t = Dk ÷ thickness in cm: 100 ÷ 0.01 cm = 100 (× 10⁻⁹ units).

mcq.q: If a lens's thickness doubles, its Dk/t
mcq.explanation: Dk/t is Dk divided by thickness, so doubling the thickness halves the transmissibility.

mcq.q: Why is a minus lens's oxygen transmissibility lower at the edge?
mcq.explanation: Minus lenses are thinnest in the centre and thicker towards the periphery, so Dk/t (Dk ÷ t) is lower there.

mcq.q: Hypoxic corneal swelling happens because

options.text: lactate builds up and draws in water
the tears evaporate from the cornea
the lens absorbs water from the cornea

mcq.explanation: With too little oxygen, the epithelium switches to anaerobic metabolism. Lactate builds up in the stroma and draws in water, so the cornea swells.

mcq.q: About how much does the cornea swell overnight without lenses?
mcq.explanation: Lower oxygen with the eyes closed causes about 3–4% corneal swelling overnight even without lenses. It clears soon after waking.

mcq.q: Open-eye oxygen at the cornea is about
mcq.explanation: With the eye open, the cornea gets oxygen from air (about 21%, around 155 mmHg). With the eye closed it drops to about 8% (around 55 mmHg) from the palpebral conjunctiva.

mcq.q: Why is oxygen supply lower when a lens wearer sleeps?

options.text: Oxygen then comes from the lid, not air
Tears stop flowing completely at night
The cornea stops using oxygen in sleep
It isn't lower when the eyes are closed

mcq.explanation: Open eye: oxygen from the air. Closed eye: from the palpebral conjunctiva, at much lower levels.

original.q: With the eye closed, oxygen comes mainly from

mcq.q: As water content rises, a hydrogel's refractive index
mcq.explanation: Water has a lower refractive index (1.333) than the polymer, so the more water a hydrogel holds, the lower its refractive index.

mcq.q: Which instrument can estimate a soft lens's water content?
mcq.explanation: Because refractive index falls predictably with water content, a hand refractometer can estimate a soft lens's water content.

mcq.q: Silicone hydrogels in the FDA system have been placed in
mcq.explanation: Silicone hydrogels don't fit the original four FDA groups, so they have been placed in a separate Group V.

mcq.q: Why do high-water lenses tear more easily?
mcq.explanation: More water means less polymer, so high-water lenses are mechanically weaker and tear or split more easily.

mcq.q: A handling (visibility) tint helps
mcq.explanation: A light handling tint makes the lens easy to see in the case or on a finger without changing eye colour.

mcq.q: Some lenses have UV-blocking classes. Class I blocks
mcq.explanation: Class I UV blockers absorb more UV (over 90% UVA and 99% UVB) than Class II (over 70% UVA and 95% UVB).

mcq.q: Which property describes a material's stiffness?
mcq.explanation: Modulus measures a material's stiffness (resistance to deformation). Higher-modulus silicone hydrogels are stiffer.

mcq.q: A lower contact angle means
mcq.explanation: The lower the contact angle, the more a liquid spreads across the surface, so wettability is better.

mcq.q: Why do pure silicone lenses (not hydrogels) have problems?

options.text: They're too cheap to make well

mcq.explanation: Pure silicone elastomer lenses let plenty of oxygen through but are very hydrophobic. They attract lipid and can bind to the eye, so they're rarely used now.

mcq.q: What are the two phases of a silicone hydrogel?

options.text: Silicone for oxygen, hydrogel for water
Glass and plastic in two layers
Only one phase throughout the lens

mcq.explanation: Silicone hydrogels combine a silicone phase, which carries oxygen, with a hydrogel phase, which gives water, softness, wettability and ion permeability for lens movement.

mcq.q: Which is a symptom of hypoxia?

options.text: Haloes and blur after long wear

mcq.explanation: Corneal oedema from hypoxia scatters light, giving haloes, blur or 'misty' vision, typically after long wearing times.

mcq.q: Which sign appears with chronic hypoxia?
mcq.explanation: Chronic hypoxia can cause limbal hyperaemia and limbal neovascularisation as vessels grow in to supply oxygen.

mcq.q: Why are dailies made from many different materials?
mcq.explanation: Daily disposable lenses come in many materials so practitioners can balance cost, comfort, oxygen supply and wettability for each patient.

mcq.q: The ISO standard for contact lens materials classification is
mcq.explanation: ISO 18369 covers contact lens terminology, classification, tolerances and testing of materials.

mcq.q: Which material property most affects lens comfort at the end of the day?
mcq.explanation: Discomfort at the end of the day is closely linked to lens surface wettability and dehydration over the wearing day.

mcq.q: Why measure Dk at eye temperature?
mcq.explanation: Dk increases with temperature, so measuring at eye temperature (about 34–35°C) gives values that match what happens on the eye.

cases.scenario: A patient wears a low-Dk hydrogel monthly lens for 14 hours a day. You find limbal redness and fine new vessels encroaching 1.5 mm into the superior cornea.
cases.question: What is the cause and what change would you make?
cases.modelAnswer: These are signs of chronic corneal hypoxia. Oxygen transmissibility (Dk/t) of a conventional hydrogel is limited by its water content and is too low for long daily wear, especially in thicker or higher-powered lenses. Refit with a silicone hydrogel, which carries oxygen through the silicone and has a much higher Dk/t, or reduce wearing time, and consider daily disposables. Record and grade the vessels, photograph if possible, and review to check that the vessels empty to ghost vessels and the redness settles.

topics.askClaude: Explain Dk vs Dk/t with an everyday analogy, then ask me 3 questions comparing hydrogel and silicone hydrogel lenses.

topics.title: Soft lens fitting assessment
topics.summary: A good soft fit centres well with full corneal coverage, moves a little on blink, and passes the push-up test with moderate resistance. Assess after the lens has settled, and always check vision with an over-refraction.
keyPoints: Let the lens settle (about 5–20 minutes) before judging the fit.
Centration: full corneal coverage in all positions of gaze, with an overlap onto the conjunctiva all round.
Movement: a small amount on blink in primary gaze (roughly 0.2–0.4 mm) and some lag on upgaze/lateral gaze.
Push-up test: push the lens up with the lower lid; it should move with moderate resistance and recentre smoothly.
Tight fit: little or no movement, conjunctival indentation/blanching at the edge, vision may clear just after a blink.
Loose fit: lots of movement, decentration, edge lift, variable vision and discomfort.
Over-refract in the trial lens, then check VA and comfort.
examTraps: Judging the fit straight after insertion, before settling.
Calling a lens 'good' because it's comfortable — tight lenses often feel comfortable at first.
Using standard sodium fluorescein with soft lenses (it stains them).

diagram.description: Front view of an eye with a soft lens edge drawn as a circle beyond the limbus. Three versions: good fit (centred, even overlap), tight (centred but conjunctival vessels compressed at the edge, no movement), loose (decentred, edge visible on the cornea when looking up).

goDeeper.heading: The push-up test
goDeeper.body: With the patient looking straight ahead, use the lower lid margin to push the lens up gently. Grade the resistance: very loose lenses move with almost no force, very tight ones won't move. Many clinicians express it as a percentage tightness, aiming for around the middle (about 50%). Note how quickly the lens recentres when released.

goDeeper.heading: Fixing a poor fit
goDeeper.body: Too tight: try a flatter base curve or a smaller diameter (or a different material/design). Too loose: try a steeper base curve or a larger diameter. Change one thing at a time and re-assess after settling.

goDeeper.heading: Over-refraction and VA
goDeeper.body: Over-refract with spheres (and JCC for torics) over the trial lens. Vision that blurs and clears with blinking suggests a fitting problem rather than a power problem. If the lens is toric, check the orientation marks and use LARS ('left add, right subtract') to correct the axis for rotation.

checklist.title: Soft lens fit assessment
steps: Wash and dry hands; check the lens isn't inside out; insert.
Wait for the lens to settle (about 5–20 minutes).
Ask about comfort and vision.
Slit lamp, diffuse light, low magnification: assess centration and coverage.
Assess movement on blink in primary gaze.
Assess lag in up gaze and lateral gaze.
Do the push-up test and grade tightness.
Look at the edge for conjunctival indentation or edge lift.
Over-refract and record VA.
Record lens details and your fit assessment, and decide on the next step.

flashcards.front: Signs of a tight soft lens
flashcards.back: Little/no movement, conjunctival indentation, vision clears briefly after a blink, may feel fine at first.

flashcards.front: Signs of a loose soft lens
flashcards.back: Excess movement, decentration, edge lift, variable vision, discomfort.
Moderate resistance (about 50% tightness) and smooth recentration.
LARS: left add, right subtract (rotation as you see it).

mcq.q: After 15 minutes a soft lens barely moves on blink and you see blanching of conjunctival vessels at the edge. Next step?

options.feedback: Yes — these are signs of a tight fit.
Tight lenses can be comfortable at first but cause problems later.

mcq.explanation: Minimal movement and edge indentation mean too tight; loosen with a flatter BOZR or smaller diameter.

mcq.q: A toric lens's orientation mark sits 10° to the right (as you look at it). The trial lens axis is 180. What axis do you order?

options.feedback: You need to compensate for the rotation.
That's a 90° change; rotation compensation is the amount seen.

mcq.explanation: LARS — left add, right subtract — as seen by the practitioner. 180 − 10 = 170.

mcq.q: Immediately after insertion, a new soft lens moves a lot and the patient is tearing. What should you do?

options.text: Change to a tighter lens now

mcq.explanation: Let the lens settle before judging fit or over-refracting.

original.q: How long should a soft lens settle before you judge the fit?

mcq.q: After settling, a soft lens barely moves on blinking and leaves a ring on the conjunctiva when removed. What's the fit, and what's one fix?

options.text: Tight: flatten the BOZR or go smaller
Inside out: flip it and retry

mcq.explanation: Little movement and conjunctival indentation suggest a tight fit.

original.q: Which sign suggests a tight soft lens?

options.text: Little or no movement with conjunctival indentation at the edge

mcq.q: In the push-up test, a good fit

options.text: moves with some resistance, then recentres
doesn't move at all when pushed
falls straight out of the eye

mcq.explanation: In a good fit the lens moves easily when pushed up with the lower lid, then recentres smoothly. No movement means tight. A lens that drops or stays decentred is loose.

mcq.q: What coverage should a soft lens give?

options.text: Full corneal coverage in all gazes

mcq.explanation: Soft lenses should cover the whole cornea plus a margin onto the conjunctiva in all directions of gaze. An exposed limbus causes irritation and desiccation.

mcq.q: Vision clears just after each blink. What does it suggest?

options.feedback: Yes: the blink briefly flexes it.
That gives variable vision too, but clearing after a blink suggests tight.

mcq.explanation: A tight lens can vault the cornea. Each blink briefly flexes it into better alignment, so vision clears for a moment and then blurs again.

mcq.q: How much movement on blink is typical for a well-fitting soft lens?

options.feedback: That's more like a rigid lens.

mcq.explanation: A well-fitting soft lens moves about 0.2–0.4 mm on each blink in primary gaze, enough for tear exchange without discomfort.

mcq.q: After assessing fit, what do you do?
mcq.explanation: Once the fit is acceptable, over-refract to fine-tune the power and record the visual acuity before you finalise the lens.

mcq.q: A soft lens decentres, moves too much and its edge stands off. What's the fault?

options.feedback: Possibly, but loose fits look like this.

mcq.explanation: Decentration, too much movement and an edge that lifts away from the conjunctiva are the signs of a loose soft lens fit.

mcq.q: How do you tighten a loose soft lens?
mcq.explanation: A steeper BOZR or a larger diameter increases the lens's sagittal depth, which tightens the fit.

mcq.q: How do you loosen a tight soft lens?
mcq.explanation: A flatter BOZR or a smaller diameter reduces the sagittal depth, which loosens the fit.

mcq.q: A toric mark rotates 10° to the left. Trial lens axis 180. What axis do you order?
mcq.explanation: Use LARS: Left Add, Right Subtract (rotation as you look at the eye). The lens rotates 10° left, so order 180 + 10 = 190, which is written as 10.

mcq.q: Why is standard fluorescein not used with soft lenses?
mcq.explanation: Soft lenses absorb sodium fluorescein and stain. High-molecular-weight fluorescein exists, but white-light assessment is standard.

mcq.q: What total diameter do most soft lenses have?
mcq.explanation: Most soft lenses are about 14.0–14.5 mm in diameter, larger than the cornea (HVID about 11.7 mm), so they overlap onto the conjunctiva.

mcq.q: You over-refract straight after inserting a trial lens and get −0.75 D. Ten minutes later it's −0.25 D. Which result should you trust?
mcq.explanation: Straight after insertion, reflex tears and lens settling change the power on the eye. Wait 10–20 minutes and trust the settled over-refraction.

original.q: When should over-refraction be done?

mcq.q: Which methods stabilise soft torics?
mcq.explanation: Soft torics are stabilised by prism ballast (a thicker base down) or by thin zones (dynamic or double-slab-off designs) that use lid pressure to hold orientation.

mcq.q: Lag on upgaze in a good soft lens fit is about
mcq.explanation: On upgaze, a well-fitting lens lags slightly, about 0.5 mm. No lag suggests tight, and a lot of lag suggests loose.

mcq.q: Which light should you use to judge soft lens fit?

options.text: White light at the slit lamp

mcq.explanation: Soft lens fit (centration, coverage, movement) is judged with diffuse white light at the slit lamp, because standard fluorescein would stain the lens.

mcq.q: What mainly decides how tight a soft lens fits?
mcq.explanation: Fit depends mainly on how the lens's sagittal depth compares with the eye's sag over the same chord. Both BOZR and diameter change sag.

mcq.q: Increasing a soft lens's total diameter makes the fit
mcq.explanation: A larger diameter increases the lens's sagittal depth relative to the eye, so the fit becomes tighter.

mcq.q: Steepening a soft lens's BOZR makes the fit
mcq.explanation: A steeper (smaller) BOZR increases the sagittal depth, which tightens the fit.

mcq.q: How much primary-gaze movement suits a soft lens?
mcq.explanation: About 0.2–0.4 mm of movement on blinking in primary gaze shows the lens isn't tight but is still stable.

mcq.q: A soft lens leaves the limbus exposed at the edge in some gazes. What's wrong?

options.text: Poor coverage: too small or off-centre
A perfect fit for that eye
The lens is fitting too tightly
The lens has been put in inside out

mcq.explanation: The cornea should be fully covered in all gazes. An exposed limbus means the lens is too small or decentred.

mcq.q: A loose soft lens typically gives
mcq.explanation: A loose lens moves and decentres after each blink, so vision fluctuates.

mcq.q: Conjunctival indentation after removing a soft lens suggests
mcq.explanation: A ring indentation on the conjunctiva after removal (sometimes with vessel blanching) shows the lens edge was pressing too hard, which means a tight fit.

mcq.q: A −2.00 DC toric rotates 10°. Roughly what residual cylinder results?
mcq.explanation: When a cylinder rotates off axis, the residual cylinder is about 2 × C × sin(θ) = 2 × 2.00 × sin 10° ≈ 0.70 DC.

mcq.q: Why check toric lens stability over several blinks?
mcq.explanation: Toric lenses only work if they settle in a stable orientation. Rotation that varies from blink to blink makes vision fluctuate.

mcq.q: Toric orientation marks are often at
mcq.explanation: Toric marks are usually at 6 o'clock or at 3 and 9 o'clock. They show orientation, not the cylinder axis itself.

mcq.q: When fitting multifocal soft lenses, you should consider
mcq.explanation: Multifocal success depends on choosing the right design and dominant-eye strategy for the patient's visual tasks, not just matching the add.

mcq.q: An inside-out soft lens often
mcq.explanation: An inside-out soft lens often shows a flared edge profile, moves more, decentres and feels less comfortable.

mcq.q: Why are single-use trial lenses preferred?
mcq.explanation: Single-use trial lenses remove the risk of cross-infection (including prions and Acanthamoeba) from reused diagnostic lenses.

mcq.q: A soft lens's TD is usually chosen at about
mcq.explanation: Soft lens diameter is usually about HVID + 2 to 3 mm, giving full corneal coverage with a conjunctival overlap.

mcq.q: A soft lens specification must include
mcq.explanation: A contact lens specification must identify the lens fully: material or brand, BOZR, total diameter, power and the prescription expiry date.

mcq.q: What's the push-up test?

options.text: Pushing it up with the lower lid
A test of the eye pressure

mcq.explanation: In the push-up test, you push the lens up with the lower lid through the lower lid margin and judge how easily it moves and how it recentres.

mcq.q: A tight lens may give clear vision just after blinking because

options.text: blinking briefly flexes or moves it
it's a perfect fit after all

mcq.explanation: A blink can briefly flex or shift a tight lens into better alignment, so vision clears just after blinking.

mcq.q: Why might a well-fitting lens later become tight?

options.text: It never becomes tight over time
The box was stored somewhere warm

mcq.explanation: Over time, dehydration, deposits or changes to the ocular surface can tighten a lens that once fitted well, which is why aftercare matters.

mcq.q: Which over-refraction result means a sphere change is needed?
mcq.explanation: If a sphere clearly improves acuity on over-refraction, the contact lens sphere power needs changing.

mcq.q: A soft toric for −2.00/−1.25 × 180 rotates 10° clockwise (to the left as you look). Which axis do you order?
mcq.explanation: LARS: the lens rotates to the left (clockwise as you look), so add: 180 + 10 = 190, which is written as 10.

mcq.q: When might you choose a toric soft lens?

options.feedback: Very low cylinder may not need it.

mcq.explanation: A toric is usually considered once uncorrected cylinder of about 0.75 DC or more noticeably reduces vision with a spherical lens.

mcq.q: Why check centration in all gaze positions?
mcq.explanation: The lens must cover the cornea in every gaze. Decentring in some gazes can expose the limbus and cause discomfort.

mcq.q: A soft lens decentres temporally. A possible fix?
mcq.explanation: Decentration usually means the fit is too loose. Tightening it with a larger diameter or steeper BOZR helps it centre.

mcq.q: Why do you re-check the fit at the first aftercare?
mcq.explanation: The fit can change after hours of wear and days of adaptation (dehydration, settling), so it is reassessed at aftercare.

mcq.q: What does a centre thickness of about 0.07 mm suggest?
mcq.explanation: Low-minus soft lenses are typically about 0.06–0.08 mm thick in the centre. Rigid lenses, sclerals and high plus lenses are much thicker.

mcq.q: Which patient is best suited to a monthly silicone hydrogel?

options.text: A full-time wearer happy with care

mcq.explanation: Reusable monthly lenses suit motivated full-time wearers who are happy to clean and store lenses properly. Dailies suit occasional wear, solution allergies or poor hygiene.

mcq.q: Which test confirms the lens isn't too loose on upgaze?
mcq.explanation: Lag on upgaze shows how much the lens slips as the eye looks up. Too much lag means the lens is loose.

mcq.q: Why give a wearing schedule?
mcq.explanation: Building up wearing time gradually lets the eye adapt, and lets you spot problems before they become serious.

mcq.q: If a lens is uncomfortable straight away, what should you check first?
mcq.explanation: Immediate discomfort usually means the lens is inside out, damaged or has debris on it, so check the lens before assuming a fit problem.

mcq.q: What does good corneal coverage prevent?

options.text: An early cataract in that eye

mcq.explanation: Full coverage stops the lens edge sitting on the cornea or leaving the limbus exposed, which causes irritation and desiccation staining.

cases.scenario: A new soft lens wearer says the lenses felt great at the trial but by the end of the day her eyes are red and vision fluctuates. At aftercare the lens doesn't move on blink.
cases.question: What's going on and what do you do?
cases.modelAnswer: A tight fit: comfortable initially but causing limbal redness, reduced tear exchange and variable vision. Remove lenses, check the cornea and conjunctiva (staining, indentation), refit with a flatter base curve or smaller diameter (or different material), and review. Reinforce wearing time and hygiene advice.

topics.askClaude: Describe 4 soft lens fits to me in words (movement, centration, push-up, edges). I'll say tight, loose or good and what to change; correct me.

topics.title: Rigid lens design and fitting
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 4 and 5 lectures: why rigid lenses, their materials and naming, back-surface design, and the fitting routine from choosing a first trial lens to assessing dynamic and static (fluorescein) fit and adjusting power.
keyPoints: Benefits: sharper stable vision, good oxygen, durability, tailoring for irregular corneas and high astigmatism, deposit resistance, long-term cost. Good candidates: motivated, moderate to high Rx, stable toricity, residual cyl under 0.75 D.

Materials: PMMA (almost no oxygen, not a GP material), CAB, silicone acrylates, fluorosilicone acrylates (Dk 40 to 100+; Menicon Z, Dk 163, approved for 30 nights). USAN names: prefix, 'focon', formulation letter, group (I none, II silicone, III both, IV fluorine), Dk band.

Design aims: match the cornea, avoid indentation, keep tears exchanging, avoid lid irritation and decentration. Designs moved from constant axial edge lift to constant axial edge clearance (about 60–80 µm).
Tricurve: BOZD = TD − 1.4; secondary curve BOZR + 1.0 mm; peripheral curve BOZR + 2.5 mm. Ideal central tear layer 15–20 µm.
First BOZR from flat K and corneal astigmatism: under 0.50 DC, 0.05 mm steeper; 0.50–1.00 DC, 0.05–0.10 mm steeper; 1.00–2.00 DC, a third of the difference steeper; over 2.00 DC, toric.
TD about 2 mm smaller than HVID (usually 8.50–10.50 mm, ideally with upper lid attachment); BOZD about 1 mm larger than the pupil in average light. Plus and high powers are made larger.

Let the lens settle 10–20 minutes. Dynamic fit: comfort, coverage, centration and movement (grade 0 = 1.1–1.5 mm). Static fit: fluorescein with cobalt blue and a yellow filter, graded by zone in each meridian.
Sagittal depth decides fit: a steeper BOZR or bigger TD makes it steeper. Each 0.05 mm steeper BOZR adds +0.25 D of tear lens, so order 0.25 D more minus (and the reverse).
A spherical lens fitted on flat K on a with-the-rule cornea shows a horizontal band of alignment with pooling above and below.
examTraps: Calling a GP lens 'hard': hard means PMMA.
Changing BOZR without adjusting power for the tear lens.
Reading a with-the-rule band of touch as a flat fit.
Over-minusing the over-refraction: check with a +1.00 blur test. Ignore cylinders under 1.00 D.

diagram.description: Three circular RGP lenses on a cornea viewed under cobalt blue. Alignment: even pale green centrally with a bright green edge band. Steep: bright green central pool with a dark ring of touch mid-periphery and narrow edge band. Flat: dark centre (touch) with wide bright green edge stand-off.

goDeeper.heading: Worked power example
goDeeper.body: Trial lens 8.00 / −2.00, over-refraction −1.50: ordering 8.00 needs −3.50. Ordering 8.10 makes the tear lens 0.50 D more minus, so order −3.00.

goDeeper.heading: Aspheric rigid lenses
goDeeper.body: Pros: better capillary attraction, less flare, no transition pressure, thinner, easier to fit, less spectacle blur. Cons: corneal asphericity is hard to measure, centration can be poor, hard to verify and modify, and optics suffer if decentred.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: reading fluorescein patterns
goDeeper.body: Steep: central pooling (sometimes a bubble) with mid-peripheral touch. Flat: dark central touch, wide edge stand-off, decentration and rocking. Alignment: thin even central fluorescein, light mid-peripheral bearing and an edge band about 0.5 mm wide.

flashcards.back: Central pooling (bright green), mid-peripheral touch ring, narrow edge band.
Central touch (dark), wide edge stand-off, decentration/rocking.
Steeper add minus, flatter add plus.

flashcards.front: BOZR change per 0.25 D tear lens
flashcards.back: About 0.05 mm.

flashcards.front: USAN stem for a rigid lens material
flashcards.back: 'focon' (soft lenses are 'filcon').

flashcards.front: First GP lens approved for 30 days' continuous wear
flashcards.back: Menicon Z (Dk 163).
Deposit-prone, scratch easily, more breakage, crazing, flexure and parameter instability.

flashcards.front: Trial lens 8.00 / −2.00, over-refraction −1.50. You order 8.10. What power?
flashcards.back: −3.00 D. −3.50 at 8.00, but the flatter BOZR makes the tear lens 0.50 D more minus.

flashcards.front: How long should a rigid trial lens settle?
flashcards.back: About 10 to 20 minutes, until watering subsides.

flashcards.front: Movement grade 0 for a rigid lens
flashcards.back: 1.1 to 1.5 mm between blinks.

mcq.q: Under cobalt blue you see a bright green central pool and a dark ring mid-peripherally. What's the fit?

options.feedback: Yes — central clearance with mid-peripheral bearing.
Alignment is a thin even layer centrally.
That's a horizontal band of touch, not a ring.

mcq.explanation: Green = tear thickness (clearance); dark = touch. A central pool means the lens is steeper than the central cornea.

mcq.q: You steepen the BOZR by 0.10 mm. What power change keeps the same over-refraction?

options.feedback: SAM: steeper add minus; 0.10 mm ≈ 0.50 D.
The tear lens power changes with BOZR.
0.10 mm ≈ 0.50 D, so −0.25 is only half.

mcq.explanation: Roughly 0.05 mm per 0.25 D. A steeper lens creates a more positive tear lens, compensated with minus.

mcq.q: Siloxane acrylate rigid lens materials have

options.text: siloxane (Si-O-Si) bonds that give momentary molecular-sized voids
options.feedback: Yes: that is how oxygen passes through by diffusion.
The backbone is acrylate (methacrylate) with siloxane groups added.
Early SAs had Dk around 10–15; high Dks came with fluorosilicone acrylates.
Silicone makes the surface more hydrophobic.
SAs are deposit-prone; adding fluorine reduced surface charge.

mcq.explanation: Siloxane (Si-O-Si) bonds leave momentary molecular-sized voids, which is how oxygen diffuses through the material.

mcq.q: Rigid contact lenses

options.text: are less likely to cause infection than soft lenses
should only be used for diseased corneas
options.feedback: They suit normal eyes too, especially astigmats and myopia control.

options.text: should only be fitted by hospital optometrists
options.feedback: They are fitted in community practice.
They last longer and are cost-effective over time.

options.text: need replacing more often than soft lenses
options.feedback: They often last a year or more.

mcq.explanation: Rigid lenses are less likely to cause infection than soft lenses.

mcq.q: The ideal tear layer thickness under the centre of a rigid lens is

options.feedback: That would start to show central pooling.
Steep, with central pooling and possible bubbles.

mcq.explanation: The ideal central tear layer under a rigid lens is about 15–20 µm.

mcq.q: What fluorescein pattern does a steep rigid lens show?

options.text: Central touch with wide edge clearance

mcq.explanation: A steep lens vaults the corneal centre, so fluorescein pools centrally. The lens bears in the mid-periphery (dark ring) with little edge clearance.

mcq.q: What total diameter suits a rigid lens for HVID 11.5 mm?

options.feedback: Yes: about 2 mm less than HVID.
Too big for a corneal lens.

mcq.explanation: Corneal rigid lenses are usually about 2 mm smaller than HVID, so for an HVID of 11.5 mm, a total diameter of about 9.50 mm.

mcq.q: What's the ideal central tear layer thickness?
mcq.explanation: An alignment fit has a thin, even central tear layer of about 15–20 µm, which shows as faint green under fluorescein. Below about 10 µm looks dark (touch).

mcq.q: Fluorescein shows a dark centre under a rigid lens and a very wide bright band at the edge. What's the fit?

options.feedback: Yes: central touch with excessive edge clearance.

mcq.explanation: Flat fits show central touch; steep fits show central pooling.

original.q: What fluorescein pattern does a flat rigid lens show?

options.text: Central touch with wide edge clearance

mcq.q: What pattern does an alignment rigid fit show?

options.text: Thin even centre, narrow edge band
A central area of dark touch

mcq.explanation: An alignment fit shows a thin even layer of fluorescein centrally and in the mid-periphery, with a narrow bright band of edge clearance.

mcq.q: Why does a rigid lens steeper than K need more minus?

options.text: It creates a positive tear lens
It has a negative tear lens

mcq.explanation: A BOZR steeper than K traps a positive tear lens (about +0.25 D per 0.05 mm), so extra minus is needed in the contact lens to offset it.

mcq.q: How does a spherical rigid lens correct corneal astigmatism?

options.text: The tear lens fills the difference
The lens bends to fit the cornea
It doesn't correct it at all
With prism built into the lens

mcq.explanation: Tears fill the space between the spherical back surface and the toric cornea. Because the tear index is close to the cornea's, this tear lens largely neutralises corneal astigmatism.

mcq.q: What does the USAN suffix '-focon' mean?
mcq.explanation: In USAN names, '-focon' marks a rigid gas permeable lens material, e.g. fluorosilicone acrylates.

mcq.q: What does the USAN suffix '-filcon' mean?
mcq.explanation: In USAN names, '-filcon' marks a soft (hydrogel or silicone hydrogel) material, e.g. 'senofilcon'.

mcq.q: A rigid lens on a cornea with 3 D of astigmatism rocks. What's the fix?
mcq.explanation: On high corneal toricity, a spherical lens bears along the flat meridian and rocks. A toric back surface matches the cornea and stabilises the fit.

mcq.q: A patient needs a rigid lens for overnight orthokeratology. Which material family suits best?
mcq.explanation: Fluorosilicone acrylates give the highest Dk rigid lenses.

original.q: Which materials give the highest Dk rigid lenses?

mcq.q: A rigid lens tucked under the upper lid is a
mcq.explanation: In a lid-attached fit, the upper part of the lens tucks under the upper lid, which holds it up and moves it with the lid. This is often more comfortable.

mcq.q: 3 and 9 o'clock staining with rigid lenses is linked to

options.text: a steep fit and nothing else

mcq.explanation: Staining at 3 and 9 o'clock comes from incomplete blinking and edge-related drying of the exposed peripheral cornea beside the lens, so edge design and blinking matter.

mcq.q: A first-choice rigid BOZR for an alignment fit is often

options.text: on flat K or slightly flatter

mcq.explanation: For an alignment fit, rigid corneal lenses usually start on flat K or slightly flatter (about 0.05–0.10 mm), depending on toricity and diameter.

mcq.q: Typical corneal rigid lens total diameters are about
mcq.explanation: Corneal rigid lenses are typically about 9.0–10.0 mm in diameter. Soft lenses are about 14 mm and sclerals larger still.

mcq.q: Why do rigid lenses have flatter peripheral curves?
mcq.explanation: Flatter peripheral curves give edge lift (edge clearance). This allows tear exchange, easier removal and comfort, and stops the edge digging in.

mcq.q: Under fluorescein, a dark area under a rigid lens means
mcq.explanation: Fluorescein looks dark where the tear layer is very thin (under about 10 µm), so dark areas mean touch or bearing.

mcq.q: How is fluorescein applied for rigid fitting?

options.text: A wet strip on the bulbar conjunctiva
Straight from the bottle onto the cornea
Injected under the lens with a needle
It isn't used for rigid fitting

mcq.explanation: A fluorescein strip moistened with saline is touched to the bulbar conjunctiva (often the lower temporal), and blinking spreads it under the lens.

mcq.q: The BOZR is 0.10 mm steeper than flat K. What tear lens forms?
mcq.explanation: Each 0.05 mm steeper than K adds about +0.25 D of tear lens, so 0.10 mm steeper gives about +0.50 D.

mcq.q: The BOZR is 0.05 mm flatter than K. Tear lens?
mcq.explanation: Fitting 0.05 mm flatter than K creates a negative tear lens of about −0.25 D.

mcq.q: Spectacle −3.00 DS (vertex negligible), BOZR on K. CL power?
mcq.explanation: A BOZR on K means no tear lens. Vertex is negligible, so the contact lens power equals the spectacle power, −3.00 D.

mcq.q: Spectacle −3.00 DS, BOZR 0.10 mm steeper than K. CL power?
mcq.explanation: 0.10 mm steeper gives a +0.50 D tear lens, so the lens needs 0.50 D more minus: −3.00 − 0.50 = −3.50 D.

mcq.q: Bubbles trapped under a steep rigid lens leaving dimples in the epithelium is called
mcq.explanation: Dimple veiling is when air bubbles trapped under a steep rigid lens press small pits into the epithelium. Fluorescein pools in them.

mcq.q: A low-riding rigid lens is often linked with
mcq.explanation: A lens that rides low often causes poor blinking over it, leading to 3 and 9 o'clock staining and discomfort.

mcq.q: When is a back-surface toric rigid lens usually considered?
mcq.explanation: Back-surface torics are usually considered once corneal astigmatism exceeds about 2.00–2.50 D, when a spherical lens won't fit or centre well.

mcq.q: A spherical rigid lens on a toric cornea may flex. What's the effect?
mcq.explanation: If a thin spherical lens flexes to match a toric cornea, the tear lens doesn't fully neutralise the corneal astigmatism, so residual astigmatism appears on over-refraction.

mcq.q: An instrument used to verify rigid BOZR is the
mcq.explanation: A radiuscope (or optical spherometer) uses the Drysdale method to measure a rigid lens's back optic zone radius.

mcq.q: Rigid lens total diameter can be checked with a
mcq.explanation: A V-gauge (or band magnifier) measures a rigid lens's total diameter: the lens is slid along a tapering channel until it stops.

mcq.q: How can a wearer remove a rigid lens without touching it?

options.text: Pull the outer lids taut and blink
Pinch it out like a soft lens
Rinse it out with tap water
Rub the eye until it moves

mcq.explanation: Pulling the outer canthus taut and blinking lets the lid margins squeeze the lens out without the finger touching the eye.

mcq.q: Rigid lens adaptation usually involves
