mcq.explanation: Rigid lenses cause noticeable lid awareness at first, so wearing time is built up gradually as the lids adapt.

mcq.q: Why does fluorine improve high-Dk rigid materials?
mcq.explanation: Adding fluorine to fluorosilicone acrylates improves wettability and deposit resistance, offsetting the drawbacks of the silicone that increases Dk.

mcq.q: A spherical rigid lens on a with-the-rule toric cornea shows which pattern?
mcq.explanation: On a WTR cornea, the flatter horizontal meridian aligns with a spherical lens (touch), while fluorescein pools above and below, giving a horizontal 'dumbbell' band of touch.

mcq.q: What does 'interpalpebral fit' mean?

options.text: It sits under the upper lid

mcq.explanation: An interpalpebral fit sits between the upper and lower lids without tucking under the upper lid, and usually uses a smaller diameter.

mcq.q: A smaller TD rigid lens tends to

options.text: sit between the lids, moving more

mcq.explanation: Smaller-diameter rigid lenses tend to sit between the lids and move more on blinking. Larger ones are more often lid-attached.

mcq.q: Which is a bitoric rigid lens?
mcq.explanation: A bitoric lens has toric back and front surfaces: the back for fit on a toric cornea and the front to correct the induced astigmatism.

mcq.q: Why is fluorescein pattern assessed after the lens has settled?

options.text: Reflex tearing first distorts the pattern

mcq.explanation: Reflex tearing after insertion thickens the tear film and makes the lens move a lot, so wait until it settles before judging the fluorescein pattern.

mcq.q: Rigid lens care usually involves

options.text: a soft lens MPS every time

mcq.explanation: Rigid lenses need a rigid lens cleaner and a conditioning (wetting and soaking) solution. Tap water must never be used, because of Acanthamoeba.

mcq.q: Why might a high-Dk rigid lens need more frequent replacement?
mcq.explanation: Higher-Dk materials are softer and less stable, so some scratch, flex and attract deposits more and need replacing more often.

mcq.q: Rigid lens power is checked with

options.text: a focimeter, back towards the stop
a radiuscope on the back surface

mcq.explanation: Rigid lens back vertex power is measured on a focimeter with the back surface against the lens stop.

mcq.q: Which feature is ideal in rigid lens movement?
mcq.explanation: A well-fitting corneal rigid lens moves smoothly by about 1–2 mm with each blink, which allows tear exchange.

mcq.q: An apical clearance fit is often used for

options.feedback: Yes, or a light three-point touch.

mcq.explanation: In keratoconus, an apical clearance fit (or light three-point touch) avoids heavy bearing on the thin, steep cone.

mcq.q: Why do rigid lenses correct corneal astigmatism better than soft spherical lenses?
mcq.explanation: A rigid lens keeps its shape and traps a tear lens that neutralises corneal astigmatism. A soft spherical lens drapes over the cornea and copies its toricity.

mcq.q: What's the risk of a very flat rigid lens?
mcq.explanation: A very flat lens bears centrally on the cornea, rocks and decentres, and can cause central staining and discomfort.

cases.scenario: A rigid lens material is labelled 'paflufocon C II 2'.
cases.question: Explain each part of the USAN name.
cases.modelAnswer: 'Paflu' is the USAN prefix (optional outside the USA). 'focon' means a rigid gas permeable material. 'C' means the third formulation of the polymer. 'II' is the group suffix: silicone but no fluorine. The final number is the Dk band: 2 is Dk 16–30 on the lecture's table. (The answer sheet says '3, Dk 31–60', which matches the lecture's own example 'paflufocon B III 3' rather than this question, so check with Dr Dutta.)

cases.scenario: Spectacle Rx RE −2.00 DS. K readings 8.30 @ 180 / 7.90 @ 90, no distortion. Tricurve trial lens 8.30 : 9.90 : −2.00 D.
cases.question: Describe (and sketch) the fluorescein pattern you would expect.
cases.modelAnswer: The cornea has 0.40 mm (about 2.25 D) with-the-rule toricity. The lens is fitted on flat K, so along the horizontal (flat) meridian it aligns, giving a dark horizontal band of alignment or light touch across the centre. In the steeper vertical meridian the cornea falls away more steeply, so fluorescein pools above and below that band, with a peripheral edge band all round: the classic with-the-rule 'dumbbell' pattern. Label the central horizontal alignment, the superior and inferior pooling, and the edge clearance.

topics.askClaude: Describe RGP fluorescein patterns to me and ask me to call each one steep, flat or alignment and what BOZR change I'd make (with SAM-FAP).

topics.title: Choosing lens power: vertex distance correction
topics.summary: A contact lens sits on the cornea, not at the spectacle plane, so higher prescriptions need converting. From the week 9 lecture: Fcl = Fsp ÷ (1 − dFsp), measure contact lens BVP with a small focimeter stop, and remember the accommodation differences between contact lenses and spectacles.
keyPoints: Vertex distance correction: Fcl = Fsp ÷ (1 − d × Fsp), with d (the BVD) in metres.
Myopes need less minus in contact lenses; hyperopes need more plus.
Measure contact lens back vertex power on a focimeter with a small aperture stop.
For a thick lens, BVP = F1 ÷ (1 − (t/n)F1) + F2.
Myopes accommodate more with contact lenses than with spectacles, so presbyopic symptoms may come sooner; hyperopes accommodate less, so they may be delayed.
Contact lenses move with the eye, so spectacle prism effects in eccentric gaze don't apply; spectacle aberrations grow with power and lens size.
For astigmatic prescriptions, convert each principal meridian, then rebuild the sphere and cylinder. Confirm the final power by over-refraction.
examTraps: Using d in millimetres instead of metres.
Getting the sign wrong for minus lenses (1 − d × (−F) = 1 + dF).
Converting the sphere and cyl separately instead of each meridian.

diagram.description: Side view: spectacle lens 12 mm in front of the cornea and a contact lens on the cornea, both focusing to the eye's far point. Labels show the vertex distance and the different powers needed (e.g. −6.00 spectacles vs −5.50 contact lens).

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: when to bother
goDeeper.body: Below about ±4.00 D the difference is under 0.25 D and usually ignored. Examples at 12 mm: −6.00 becomes about −5.50; +6.00 becomes about +6.50.

flashcards.back: Fc = F / (1 − dF), d in metres.

flashcards.front: When to compensate for vertex distance
flashcards.back: Prescriptions above about ±4.00 D.
About −5.50 D.
About +6.50 D.

mcq.q: Spectacle Rx −10.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?

options.feedback: Myopes need less minus in contact lenses, not more.
At this power vertex distance matters a lot.

mcq.explanation: Fc = F ÷ (1 − dF) = −10 ÷ (1 + 0.012 × 10) = −10 ÷ 1.12 ≈ −8.93 D, so order −9.00 D. Minus lenses need less power closer to the eye.

mcq.q: Spectacle Rx −5.00/−2.00 × 180 at 12 mm. What's the approximate contact lens Rx?
mcq.explanation: Convert each principal meridian for vertex distance, then rebuild the sphere and cylinder.

original.q: How should you convert −5.00/−2.00 × 180 for a contact lens?

options.text: Convert each principal meridian, then rebuild sphere and cylinder

options.feedback: The cylinder isn't a meridian power on its own.
The strongest meridian is −7.00 D, well above ±4.00.

original.explanation: Work out each meridian's power (here −5.00 and −7.00), convert both, then turn them back into sphere/cyl form.

mcq.q: A spectacle Rx of −8.00 D at 12 mm. Approximately what contact lens power?
mcq.explanation: Fc = F ÷ (1 − dF) = −8.00 ÷ (1 − 0.012 × −8.00) = −8.00 ÷ 1.096 ≈ −7.30 D, so order −7.25 D. Minus lenses need less power closer to the eye.

mcq.q: A spectacle Rx of +8.00 D at 12 mm. Approximately what contact lens power?
mcq.explanation: Fc = +8.00 ÷ (1 − 0.012 × 8.00) = +8.00 ÷ 0.904 ≈ +8.85 D, so order +8.75 D. Plus lenses need more power when moved closer to the eye.

mcq.q: Spectacle Rx −9.00 D at 12 mm. Which contact lens power is closest?
mcq.explanation: Myopes need less minus in contact lenses than in spectacles.

original.q: Myopes need what compared with their spectacles?

mcq.q: A −8.00 D myope switches to contact lenses at 43 and soon needs reading glasses, though her friend in glasses doesn't yet. Why?

options.text: She must accommodate more in CLs
Her contact lenses are too weak

mcq.explanation: Myopes accommodate more with contact lenses than with spectacles.

original.q: Why may a myope switching to contact lenses need reading glasses sooner?

options.text: They accommodate more with contact lenses than with spectacles

mcq.q: For an astigmatic Rx, how do you correct for vertex distance?
mcq.explanation: Vertex correction isn't linear, so convert the power in each principal meridian separately, then rebuild the sphere and cylinder from the two results.

mcq.q: A soft lens on a focimeter gives a fuzzy, unstable reading. What should you use?

options.text: A small stop, lens blotted, back to it
The front surface to the stop

mcq.explanation: Measure contact lens back vertex power with a small aperture stop.

original.q: How should contact lens back vertex power be measured on a focimeter?

options.text: With the front surface against the stop

mcq.q: A spectacle Rx of −3.50 D at 12 mm. Do you need to adjust the contact lens power?
mcq.explanation: Below about ±4.00 D the vertex change is under 0.25 D and usually ignored.

original.q: Roughly below what power is the vertex correction usually ignored?

options.feedback: Yes: the difference is under 0.25 D.
Correction starts mattering well above this.
It usually is at low powers.

mcq.q: In the formula Fcl = Fsp ÷ (1 − dFsp), what units is d in?
mcq.explanation: Power is in dioptres (1/metres), so d must be in metres: 12 mm is 0.012.

mcq.q: Spectacle Rx −6.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
mcq.explanation: −6.00 ÷ (1 + 0.072) ≈ −5.60 D, so the nearest available power is −5.50 D. Myopes need less minus at the cornea.

mcq.q: Spectacle Rx +6.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
mcq.explanation: +6.00 ÷ (1 − 0.072) ≈ +6.47 D, so +6.50 D. Hyperopes need more plus at the cornea.

mcq.q: Spectacle Rx −12.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
mcq.explanation: −12.00 ÷ (1 + 0.144) ≈ −10.49 D, so −10.50 D. The difference grows quickly at high powers.

mcq.q: Spectacle Rx +12.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
Spectacle −4.00/−2.00 × 180 at 12 mm. Approximate CL Rx?
mcq.explanation: The meridians are −4.00 (at 180) and −6.00 (at 90). These convert to about −3.82 and −5.60 D, giving roughly −3.75 / −1.75 × 180. The cylinder shrinks as well as the sphere.

mcq.q: Hyperopes switching to contact lenses need
mcq.explanation: Moving a plus lens closer to the eye reduces its effective power, so hyperopes need more plus in contact lenses than in spectacles.

mcq.q: A hyperope switching from glasses to CLs uses
mcq.explanation: Compared with spectacles, contact lenses lower the near accommodative demand for hyperopes and raise it for myopes.

mcq.q: How should a contact lens be placed on a focimeter?
mcq.explanation: Back vertex power is measured with the back surface against the focimeter stop. Blot the lens dry first so surface liquid doesn't distort the reading.

mcq.q: Why don't contact lenses cause prism when looking down?
mcq.explanation: Contact lenses move with the eye, so the line of sight stays near the optical centre and no prism is induced in down-gaze, unlike spectacles.

mcq.q: Why do high myopes often see things bigger in contact lenses?

options.text: A different VA chart is used

mcq.explanation: Minus spectacle lenses minify the image because of their distance from the eye. At the cornea, contact lenses minify much less, so high myopes see things larger and often with better acuity.

mcq.q: Spectacle −5.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
Spectacle +5.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
Spectacle −7.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
Spectacle +10.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
Spectacle −15.00 D at 12 mm. Nearest CL power?
Spectacle −8.00 D at 14 mm. Nearest CL power?
mcq.explanation: With d = 0.014 m: −8.00 ÷ (1 + 0.112) ≈ −7.19 D, so −7.25 D. A longer vertex distance means a bigger change.

mcq.q: Spectacle +14.00 D at 12 mm (an aphakic patient). Approximate CL power?
mcq.explanation: +14.00 ÷ (1 − 0.168) ≈ +16.83 D, so about +16.75 to +17.00 D. Aphakic powers change a lot.

mcq.q: Spectacle −2.00/−3.00 × 90 at 12 mm. Approximate CL Rx?

options.feedback: Correct for vertex in the strong meridian.

mcq.explanation: The meridians are −2.00 (at 90) and −5.00 (at 180). These convert to about −1.95 and −4.71 D, giving roughly −2.00 / −2.75 × 90.

mcq.q: Ocular refraction is
mcq.explanation: Ocular refraction is the correction needed at the corneal plane. It differs from the spectacle Rx by the vertex effect.

mcq.q: Corrected myopes in spectacles get which prism effect at near?
mcq.explanation: As a myope converges to read through minus spectacles, the eyes look nasal to the optical centres. This gives base-in prism, which reduces the convergence needed.

mcq.q: A myope switching to CLs needs to

options.text: converge and focus a little more

mcq.explanation: Compared with spectacles, myopes in contact lenses lose the base-in prism and the reduced accommodative demand, so they must converge and accommodate a little more at near.

mcq.q: A hyperope switching to CLs at near needs to

options.text: focus and converge a little less

mcq.explanation: Plus spectacles give hyperopes base-out prism and a higher accommodative demand at near. In contact lenses both fall, so they accommodate and converge a little less.

mcq.q: Over-refraction is done

options.text: with the lens on the eye

mcq.explanation: Over-refraction is done with the contact lens in place, using trial lenses in front of it to find any residual correction.

mcq.q: A soft lens over-refraction is +0.50 DS. The lens is −3.00 D. New lens?
mcq.explanation: Over-refraction adds to the lens power: −3.00 + 0.50 = −2.50 D.

mcq.q: A soft lens over-refraction is −0.75 DS with a −4.00 D lens. New lens power?
mcq.explanation: Over-refraction adds to the lens power: −4.00 + (−0.75) = −4.75 D.

mcq.q: Why is high-power over-refraction itself vertex-sensitive?

options.text: The trial lens sits away too

mcq.explanation: A high-power over-refraction lens also sits about 12 mm in front of the eye, so its effective power at the cornea differs and must be vertex-corrected too.

mcq.q: When do you not need to correct for vertex distance?
mcq.explanation: Below about ±4.00 D the vertex change is under 0.25 D, so it can usually be ignored.

mcq.q: For rigid lenses on a toric cornea, the vertex-corrected cylinder

options.text: may be neutralised by the tear lens
is always added to the lens

mcq.explanation: On a rigid lens, the tear lens can neutralise the corneal component of a vertex-corrected cylinder. Only residual cylinder needs correcting in the lens.

mcq.q: Back vertex power of a CL describes its power
mcq.explanation: Back vertex power is the lens's power measured from its back surface, the surface that sits on the eye.

mcq.q: Why should spectacles and CLs never simply share the same Rx in high myopia?
mcq.explanation: At high powers, the change in vertex distance from spectacle plane to cornea alters the effective power a lot, so each correction needs its own power.

mcq.q: A −10.00 D myope moves from spectacles to CLs. VA may improve because
mcq.explanation: Minus spectacles minify the retinal image. Contact lenses at the cornea minify much less, so the image is larger and acuity may improve.

mcq.q: A +10.00 D hyperope moves from spectacles to CLs. They notice
mcq.explanation: Plus spectacles magnify. Contact lenses at the cornea magnify much less, so things look smaller than they did in glasses.

mcq.q: Using Fcl = Fsp ÷ (1 − dFsp), what CL power matches +6.00 D spectacles at 12 mm?
mcq.explanation: Hyperopes need more plus in contact lenses than in spectacles.

original.q: Which formula gives the CL power?

mcq.q: In that formula, d = 12 mm is entered as
mcq.explanation: Vergence formulas use metres (dioptres are per metre), so 12 mm goes in as 0.012.

mcq.q: Why do high myopes in CLs need reading glasses earlier?
mcq.explanation: Myopes have a higher accommodative demand at near in contact lenses than in minus spectacles, so presbyopic symptoms can appear sooner.

mcq.q: A spectacle −4.25 D Rx at 12 mm. CL power?
mcq.explanation: −4.25 ÷ (1 + 0.051) ≈ −4.04 D, so −4.00 D is the closest step.

mcq.q: A spectacle +4.25 D Rx at 12 mm. CL power?
Spectacle −6.00/−1.00 × 180 at 12 mm. Approximate soft toric CL Rx?
mcq.explanation: The meridians are −6.00 and −7.00. These convert to about −5.60 and −6.46 D. The sphere and cylinder both reduce, and −5.50 / −0.75 × 180 is the closest option.

mcq.q: Spherical equivalent soft lenses for low cylinder use
mcq.explanation: A spherical-equivalent lens uses the sphere plus half the cylinder, which places the circle of least confusion on the retina for low astigmatism.

mcq.q: Which CL design can correct astigmatism without a toric surface?
mcq.explanation: A spherical rigid lens keeps its shape, and the tear lens beneath it neutralises corneal astigmatism, so no toric surface is needed.

cases.scenario: A patient's spectacle prescription is −8.00 DS at a vertex distance of 12 mm. They want soft contact lenses.
cases.question: What contact lens power do you order?
cases.modelAnswer: Correct for vertex distance: Fc = F ÷ (1 − dF) = −8.00 ÷ (1 − (0.012 × −8.00)) = −8.00 ÷ 1.096 = −7.30 D, so order −7.25 D. A minus lens moved closer to the eye needs less minus, and a plus lens needs more plus. The correction matters for powers of about ±4.00 D and above. With astigmatism, correct each principal meridian separately and then work out the new sphere and cylinder.

topics.askClaude: Give me 6 vertex distance conversions (including two astigmatic ones), let me work them out, then show the full working.

topics.title: Care regimes, hygiene and patient instruction
topics.summary: Most serious contact lens problems come from how lenses are handled, cleaned and stored. Good teaching — insertion, removal, cleaning, case care and 'when to take lenses out' — is part of the fit, not an afterthought.
keyPoints: Wash hands with soap and dry them thoroughly before handling lenses.
Never expose lenses or cases to tap water, swimming pools, showers or hot tubs (Acanthamoeba risk).
Multipurpose solutions: rub and rinse (even if labelled 'no rub'), use fresh solution every time, never top up.
Hydrogen peroxide systems must be fully neutralised before wear (follow the recommended time).
Clean the case, leave it to air-dry face down, and replace it regularly (at least monthly or as advised).
Daily disposables avoid cases and solutions — a good option for many patients.
Don't sleep in lenses unless prescribed for it. If eyes aren't comfortable, seeing well and looking white, take lenses out and get advice.
examTraps: Saying 'no-rub' solutions don't need rubbing — rubbing removes more microbes and deposits.
Forgetting to mention water exposure when teaching care.
Not explaining what to do in an emergency (red, painful eye).

diagram.description: Soft lens balanced on a fingertip, viewed side-on. Correct orientation: a smooth bowl with edges pointing up. Inside out: the edges flare outwards like a saucer. Inset: 'taco test' — pinching the lens gently; edges curl inwards when correct.

goDeeper.heading: Teaching insertion and removal
goDeeper.body: Insertion: lens on the dry tip of the index finger, hold the upper lid by the lashes and pull the lower lid down, look up (or straight ahead) and place the lens on the eye, then look around and blink. Removal (soft): look up, slide the lens down onto the white of the eye with the index finger, pinch it off with thumb and finger. Do the right lens first every time to avoid mix-ups.

goDeeper.heading: Why water matters
goDeeper.body: Acanthamoeba lives in tap water and can bind to lenses and cases. Acanthamoeba keratitis is rare but very painful and hard to treat. That's why lenses, cases and solution bottles should never meet water, and lenses shouldn't be worn swimming (or should be daily disposables thrown away straight after, ideally with goggles).

goDeeper.heading: Compliance
goDeeper.body: Many wearers don't follow every instruction. Keep advice short and specific, demonstrate it, give written instructions, check understanding at each aftercare and ask open questions ('Talk me through what you do when you take your lenses out at night').

checklist.title: Teaching a new soft lens wearer
steps: Wash and dry hands; keep nails short and clean.
Check the lens isn't inside out (bowl shape or taco test).
Insert: hold lids, look up or ahead, place lens, blink and look around.
Check comfort and vision.
Remove: look up, slide down onto the sclera, pinch off.
Explain cleaning (rub and rinse), fresh solution each time, no topping up.
Explain case care and replacement.
Explain no water exposure and no sleeping in lenses (unless prescribed).
Agree a wearing schedule and aftercare date.
Explain emergency advice: red, painful or blurry → lenses out, seek help.
Give written instructions and record what you taught.

flashcards.back: Rubbing removes more microbes and deposits.
Tap water, pools, hot tubs, showers.
Rinse with solution, air-dry face down, replace regularly.
If not comfortable, seeing well and looking white — lenses out and seek advice.

mcq.q: A wearer rinses her case with tap water each morning. Biggest concern?

options.feedback: Yes — tap water is the classic source.
Possible, but infection risk is the key concern.

mcq.explanation: Cases should be rinsed with fresh solution and air-dried; tap water introduces Acanthamoeba and other organisms.

mcq.q: What must happen before lenses stored in hydrogen peroxide are inserted?

options.text: Full neutralisation for the recommended time
options.feedback: Right — unneutralised peroxide stings and damages the epithelium.

mcq.explanation: Peroxide systems disinfect well but must be neutralised (e.g. with a catalytic disc) for the full time stated.

mcq.q: A wearer asks if it's fine to rinse their lens case with tap water if they dry it afterwards. What do you say?

options.text: Yes, as long as it's dried
Yes, if the water is filtered
Only if the water is very hot

mcq.explanation: Lenses and cases should never meet tap water, pools, showers or hot tubs.

original.q: Which water exposure is safe for contact lenses or cases?

options.text: None: never tap water, pools, showers or hot tubs

mcq.q: Which is wrong advice for a multipurpose solution user?

options.text: Top up yesterday's solution to save money
Rub and rinse even if labelled 'no rub'

mcq.explanation: Rub and rinse, use fresh solution every time and never top up.

original.q: How should multipurpose solution be used?

options.text: Rub and rinse, fresh solution every time, never top up

mcq.q: What must happen with a hydrogen peroxide system before wear?
mcq.explanation: Un-neutralised 3% hydrogen peroxide causes severe stinging and epithelial damage, so neutralisation must be complete before the lenses go in.

mcq.q: How should a lens case be cared for?

options.text: Washed in tap water and closed up

mcq.explanation: Cases develop biofilm. Rinse with fresh solution (never water), air-dry face down with the caps off, and replace at least monthly.

mcq.q: A patient with a solution allergy wants to keep wearing contact lenses. Which option avoids solutions entirely?
mcq.explanation: Daily disposables are thrown away each night, so no case or solution touches the eye. That removes the allergy trigger.

original.q: Which modality avoids cases and solutions entirely?

mcq.q: What should a patient do if an eye isn't comfortable, seeing well and looking white?

options.text: Take the lenses out and seek advice
Keep wearing and see if it settles
Use any eye drops at home

mcq.explanation: Use the rule 'Look good, feel good, see well?'. If any of these fail, the wearer should remove the lenses and seek advice promptly, because infection can progress quickly.

mcq.q: A new wearer moisturises their hands then handles their lenses. What's the problem?
mcq.explanation: Wash hands with soap and dry them thoroughly before handling lenses.

original.q: What's the first step before handling lenses?

options.text: Wash hands with soap and dry them thoroughly

mcq.q: Why is sleeping in daily-wear lenses risky?
mcq.explanation: Sleeping in lenses not approved for overnight wear raises the risk of microbial keratitis many times over.

mcq.q: Should lenses be rubbed even with a 'no-rub' solution?
mcq.explanation: Rubbing and rinsing removes deposits and microbes far better than soaking alone, even with 'no-rub' solutions.

mcq.q: How often should a lens case be replaced?
mcq.explanation: Cases build up biofilm over time, so they should be replaced at least monthly (often with each new bottle).

mcq.q: A wearer who showers in their lenses develops severe pain out of proportion to the signs. Which organism should you suspect?
mcq.explanation: Acanthamoeba lives in tap water and can bind to lenses and cases.

original.q: Which organism is especially linked to tap water exposure?

mcq.q: Topping up old solution in the case is
mcq.explanation: Topping up dilutes the disinfectant and leaves contaminated solution in the case, so always discard old solution and use fresh.

mcq.q: Hydrogen peroxide disinfection uses what concentration?
mcq.explanation: Peroxide systems use 3% hydrogen peroxide, which is then neutralised to water and oxygen before wear.

mcq.q: How is the case best dried?

options.text: Rinsed with solution, air-dried face down
Wiped dry with a bathroom towel
Rinsed under the tap, then closed
Left full of solution until next use

mcq.explanation: Rinse the case with fresh solution and leave it to air-dry face down with the caps off. Towels and tap water introduce microbes.

mcq.q: What does the platinum disc in a peroxide system do?
mcq.explanation: The platinum catalyst disc breaks hydrogen peroxide down into water and oxygen, which neutralises it in one-step systems.

mcq.q: Is showering in lenses safe?
mcq.explanation: Tap water can carry Acanthamoeba, so showering in lenses is best avoided. If unavoidable, keep the eyes closed.

mcq.q: What should a wearer use for swimming?

options.text: Dailies under goggles, thrown away after

mcq.explanation: Water can carry Acanthamoeba, so the safest option is daily disposables under watertight goggles, discarded straight after swimming.

mcq.q: Why must wearers never use saliva to wet lenses?
mcq.explanation: Saliva is full of bacteria and isn't sterile, so it should never be used to wet or clean lenses.

mcq.q: Multipurpose solutions contain
mcq.explanation: Multipurpose solutions combine a disinfectant, surfactant cleaner, buffers and wetting agents for cleaning, rinsing, disinfecting and storing.

mcq.q: Which is a common MPS disinfectant?
mcq.explanation: Common MPS disinfectants include PHMB (polyhexanide) and Polyquad (polyquaternium-1), often alongside Aldox.

mcq.q: How long must lenses usually soak in MPS?
mcq.explanation: Disinfection needs the full soak time on the product label, typically 4–6 hours or overnight.

mcq.q: Why can't saline be used to disinfect lenses?
mcq.explanation: Saline only rinses and stores lenses. It contains no disinfectant, so it can't kill microbes.

mcq.q: A wearer inserts a lens straight from peroxide. What happens?
mcq.explanation: Peroxide that hasn't been neutralised causes intense stinging, redness and epithelial damage.

mcq.q: Should you switch solutions without advice?
mcq.explanation: Solutions can interact with certain lens materials, causing staining or discomfort, so changes should be made on professional advice.

mcq.q: Many solutions should be discarded how long after opening?

options.text: As the bottle says, often ~90 days

mcq.explanation: Once opened, solutions can become contaminated, so discard them by the date on the bottle, often about 90 days.

mcq.q: When should lenses go in relative to make-up?

options.text: Lenses in first, out before removal
Lenses in after make-up goes on
It doesn't matter in which order

mcq.explanation: Put lenses in before make-up so it can't get onto them, and take them out before removing make-up.

mcq.q: How should hands be dried before handling lenses?
mcq.explanation: Wash hands and dry them on a clean, lint-free towel so fibres and microbes don't transfer to the lenses.

mcq.q: How long should each lens be rubbed during cleaning?
mcq.explanation: Follow the product instructions, usually about 10–20 seconds of rubbing per side, then rinse.

mcq.q: What is a biofilm in a lens case?
mcq.explanation: A biofilm is a slimy layer of microbes stuck to the case. It protects them from disinfectants, which is why cases must be cleaned and replaced.

mcq.q: Why should lenses be replaced on schedule?
mcq.explanation: Lenses build up deposits and lose surface quality over time, so replacing them on schedule keeps them comfortable and lowers complication risk.

mcq.q: What should a wearer do if they have a cold or flu?
mcq.explanation: Illness, dehydration and eye rubbing increase the risk of complications, so wearers should consider switching to spectacles until they recover.

mcq.q: What should a wearer carry when travelling?

options.text: A bottle of tap water to rinse

mcq.explanation: Carry spare lenses, a case, solution and spectacles, so lenses can be removed or replaced safely wherever you are.

mcq.q: Hot tubs and lenses

options.text: a risk: avoid, or goggles and dailies
a good way to clean lenses

mcq.explanation: Hot tubs can harbour Acanthamoeba and Pseudomonas, so avoid wearing lenses in them, or use goggles and daily disposables.

mcq.q: Home-made saline is dangerous because
mcq.explanation: Home-made saline isn't sterile and has been linked to Acanthamoeba keratitis.

mcq.q: Why should nails be kept short for handling lenses?

options.text: To avoid tearing lenses or scratches
To save time when handling lenses
There's no real reason for it

mcq.explanation: Long or sharp nails can tear soft lenses or scratch the eye during insertion and removal.

mcq.q: How much does overnight wear raise the risk of microbial keratitis?
mcq.explanation: Overnight wear raises the risk of microbial keratitis several times (around 5 or more times) compared with daily wear.

mcq.q: Which is a 'two-step' peroxide system?
mcq.explanation: In two-step peroxide systems, lenses are disinfected in peroxide and then neutralised separately (e.g. with a tablet). One-step systems do both in one case.

mcq.q: Rigid lenses should be stored in
mcq.explanation: Rigid lenses are stored in a rigid conditioning solution that disinfects and wets the surface. Never use water or saliva.

mcq.q: Hairspray should be used

options.text: before lenses go in, eyes shut

mcq.explanation: Apply hairspray before inserting lenses, with the eyes closed, so the spray can't coat the lenses.

mcq.q: Why must cases be air dried with caps off?
mcq.explanation: Damp, closed cases let microbes and biofilm grow, so air-dry the case with the caps off.

mcq.q: Which wearer is at highest risk of microbial keratitis?

options.text: One who sleeps in daily-wear lenses and smokes
A daily disposable wearer who follows advice
A rigid wearer who follows advice

mcq.explanation: Overnight wear of lenses not designed for it is the biggest risk factor, and smoking adds further risk.

mcq.q: Enzyme cleaners were used to remove
mcq.explanation: Enzyme tablets broke down protein deposits (mainly lysozyme) on reusable lenses. They're less used now that lenses are replaced more often.

mcq.q: What's the risk of buying lenses from unregulated online sellers?

options.text: None: online is just as safe

mcq.explanation: Buying without professional supervision means fits and aftercare aren't checked, which is linked to more complications.

mcq.q: Patients should remove lenses and seek advice if

options.text: the eye is red, painful or blurred
it's the end of the working week
they feel tired in the evening

mcq.explanation: A red, painful eye or blurred vision could mean infection, so remove the lenses and seek advice the same day.

mcq.q: Why are dailies good for allergy sufferers?

options.text: No build-up of deposits or solutions

mcq.explanation: A fresh lens every day means no deposit or allergen build-up and no exposure to care solutions, which helps allergy sufferers.

mcq.q: Water exposure is risky mainly because of
mcq.explanation: Tap, pool and sea water can contain Acanthamoeba and bacteria that cling to lenses, so water exposure is a major infection risk.

mcq.q: A wearer drops a monthly lens on the bathroom floor. What should they do?

options.text: Disinfect it fully, or replace it

mcq.explanation: A dropped lens is contaminated. Clean, rub and fully disinfect it before wear, or replace it. Never rinse it under the tap.

mcq.q: Which advice reduces the risk of solution contamination?

options.text: Don't touch the tip; keep it capped
Leave the cap off to air

mcq.explanation: Don't let the bottle tip touch anything, and keep it capped, so the solution stays sterile.

cases.scenario: A reusable soft lens wearer says they top up the solution in the case instead of replacing it, and rinse the case with tap water.
cases.question: What are the risks and what would you tell them?
cases.modelAnswer: Topping up dilutes the disinfectant and leaves it ineffective, and tap water can carry Acanthamoeba, which causes a painful, sight-threatening keratitis. Advise: wash and dry hands first; rub and rinse lenses with fresh solution; discard all solution from the case every day and never top up; rinse the case with solution, not water, and leave it open to air dry; replace the case at least monthly; no water contact, so no swimming or showering in lenses; and never sleep in lenses unless prescribed. Remove lenses and seek advice urgently for a red, painful or blurry eye. Daily disposables may suit them better.

topics.askClaude: Be a new contact lens wearer who's a bit careless. Let me teach you insertion, removal and care, and tell me which important points I forgot.

topics.title: Aftercare and complications
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 10 lecture: about a third of wearers have some adverse event. Know the microbes involved, how lens wear affects defences, and how to recognise and manage microbial keratitis, the inflammatory and mechanical events, and contact lens dry eye.
keyPoints: Lens wear alters epithelial function (Dk/t dependent) and lowers PMNs and sIgA; most adverse responses follow bacterial colonisation of lenses. Daily wear increases lid and conjunctival bacteria, partly from the case.
Gram-positive (e.g. Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Corynebacterium) versus Gram-negative (e.g. Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Moraxella), which have an outer membrane.
Hypoxic changes: microcysts, vacuoles, bullae, oedema, neovascularisation, endothelial blebs and polymegethism.

Presumed MK: stromal infiltrate over 1 mm, more than mild pain, plus AC reaction, mucopurulent discharge or a positive culture. About 1–2 per 10,000 daily wearers a year; about 20 per 10,000 with overnight wear. Risks: hand hygiene, overnight wear, smoking, water, male sex.

MK management: hand hygiene, replacement and compliance, no overnight wear, early presentation; treatment with antimicrobials, cycloplegic, lubricants and later steroids. Daily disposables don't cut the absolute risk but cases are milder.

CLPU: single round peripheral infiltrate up to 2 mm with staining. CLARE: diffuse peripheral infiltration with small infiltrates, staining uncommon. IK: anterior stromal infiltrates with staining. CIEs: 0–0.4% a year in daily disposables, 2.5–7% with overnight reusables.
Mechanical: CLPC (papillae on the upper tarsus, more with non-ionic hydrogels, helped by frequent replacement), SEAL (grey-white superior arc), erosion (full-thickness epithelial loss).

Contact lens dry eye: CLIDE (symptoms only with lenses) or CLADE (pre-existing). Rule out other causes, then change care system, go daily disposable, change material or design, add lubricants, punctal plugs or omega-3, avoid harsh environments.
examTraps: Under-referring: pain plus an epithelial defect plus an infiltrate is presumed MK.
Confusing CLARE (no staining, after overnight wear) with MK.
Thinking daily disposables remove MK risk.

diagram.description: Three corneas side by side. MK: large central/paracentral grey-white infiltrate with stained epithelial defect, hypopyon in the AC. CLPU: small round peripheral infiltrate with a small stained defect. CLARE: scattered small peripheral infiltrates, red eye, no defect.
labels: MK: large, central, epithelial defect, AC reaction

goDeeper.heading: Steering high-risk wearers
goDeeper.body: Avoid overnight wear; peroxide systems help. A young man with past CIEs or blepharitis, or someone with a high Rx, should be steered towards daily disposables.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: Acanthamoeba
goDeeper.body: Acanthamoeba keratitis causes pain out of proportion to the signs, a ring infiltrate and radial keratoneuritis, and is linked to water exposure. Treat any lens-related infiltrate with an epithelial defect as MK until proven otherwise.

flashcards.back: Pain, photophobia, discharge, central/paracentral infiltrate with epithelial defect, AC reaction.
Sleeping in lenses (usually wakes with a painful red eye).
Small (<2 mm), round, peripheral, with a small epithelial defect.
Papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva (evert the lid).

flashcards.front: Effects of lens wear on host defences
flashcards.back: Altered epithelial function (Dk/t dependent), fewer PMNs, less sIgA.

flashcards.front: Do daily disposables reduce MK risk?
flashcards.back: Not the absolute risk, but cases tend to be less severe with less vision loss.

mcq.q: A monthly SiHy wearer who swims in her lenses has severe pain, a ring-shaped infiltrate and relatively few signs for the pain. Most likely diagnosis?

options.feedback: Yes — water exposure, pain out of proportion, ring infiltrate.
CLARE follows overnight wear and has no ring infiltrate.
CLPU is small, peripheral and mildly uncomfortable.
GPC affects the upper tarsal conjunctiva, not the cornea.

mcq.explanation: Acanthamoeba keratitis is classically linked to water and causes pain out of proportion to signs. It's an emergency.

mcq.q: Which finding most strongly suggests MK rather than a sterile infiltrate?

options.text: Large central infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect and AC cells
options.feedback: Right — central, large, staining, with AC reaction.

options.text: Several tiny peripheral infiltrates with no staining
options.feedback: That's more typical of a sterile response (e.g. CLARE).

mcq.explanation: Size, central location, epithelial breakdown, pain and AC activity point towards infection.

mcq.q: Which statement about Gram-positive bacteria is wrong?

options.text: They have a thick peptidoglycan wall
They stain purple with Gram stain

mcq.explanation: Gram-negative bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas) have an outer membrane; Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall.

original.q: Which is NOT present in a Gram-positive bacterial cell wall?

options.feedback: Yes: only Gram-negative bacteria have one.
Gram-positive walls have a thick peptidoglycan layer.

mcq.q: 'Arc-shaped, greyish-white peripheral lesion in the superior cornea with staining and surrounding diffuse infiltration' describes

options.feedback: Diffuse peripheral infiltration in a red eye.
Painful, with an ulcer over 1 mm.

mcq.explanation: A SEAL is a mechanical lesion: a stiff lens pressing under the upper lid leaves an arc of staining at about 10–2 o'clock. Changing the lens material or design usually fixes it.

mcq.q: A lens wearer has a 0.5 mm peripheral infiltrate, mild discomfort, no discharge and a quiet AC. Does it meet the criteria for presumed microbial keratitis?

options.text: No: it needs over 1 mm and more signs
Only if the lesion is central
Only if they sleep in lenses

mcq.explanation: Presumed MK: stromal infiltrate over 1 mm, more than mild pain, plus AC reaction, mucopurulent discharge or a positive culture. Still review it carefully.

original.q: What defines presumed microbial keratitis?

options.text: Stromal infiltrate over 1 mm, more than mild pain, and AC reaction, discharge or a positive culture
Any red eye in a lens wearer

mcq.q: A soft lens wearer develops rapid keratitis with mucopurulent discharge. Which organism is most likely, and what type is it?
mcq.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the commonest cause of contact lens microbial keratitis and is Gram-negative.

original.q: Which bacterium causing keratitis is Gram-negative?

mcq.q: Which lens choice suits a young man with past infiltrative events and blepharitis?
mcq.explanation: Daily disposables cut deposit build-up and remove care solutions from the picture, which lowers the risk of infiltrative events, especially with blepharitis.

mcq.q: A patient's eyes feel dry only when wearing lenses, and fine in glasses. Which term fits?

options.text: CLADE: dry eye made worse by lenses

mcq.explanation: CLIDE symptoms occur only with lenses; CLADE is pre-existing dry eye aggravated by lenses.

original.q: CLIDE differs from CLADE how?

options.text: CLIDE symptoms only occur with lenses; CLADE is pre-existing dry eye

mcq.q: Giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva of a lens wearer suggest
mcq.explanation: Large papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva in a lens wearer are the hallmark of contact lens papillary conjunctivitis (CLPC).

mcq.q: Which organism most often causes contact lens microbial keratitis?
mcq.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a Gram-negative bacterium, is the most common cause of contact lens-related microbial keratitis.

mcq.q: A wearer has severe pain but only subtle corneal signs, with radial lines along the corneal nerves. Most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Acanthamoeba causes pain out of proportion to the signs, often with radial keratoneuritis.

original.q: Severe pain out of proportion to signs, with radial keratoneuritis, suggests

mcq.q: What is CLARE?

options.text: An acute red eye after sleeping in lenses
A chronic dry eye from lens wear
A type of extended wear lens

mcq.explanation: CLARE (contact lens acute red eye) is a sudden red, uncomfortable eye on waking after sleeping in lenses, often with small peripheral infiltrates. It is linked to Gram-negative bacterial toxins.

mcq.q: Corneal neovascularisation from hypoxia is best managed by
mcq.explanation: Neovascularisation is driven by chronic hypoxia, so manage it by increasing oxygen supply (higher-Dk materials) and reducing wearing time.

mcq.q: After switching to a high-Dk lens, microcysts may

options.text: rise for a while, then clear

mcq.explanation: After switching to a high-Dk lens, microcysts often increase for a week or so as the epithelium recovers, then gradually clear over a few months.

mcq.q: Striae appear at about what level of corneal swelling?
mcq.explanation: Vertical striae in the posterior stroma appear at about 5% corneal swelling, and folds at about 8% or more.

mcq.q: Endothelial polymegethism is associated with
mcq.explanation: Variation in endothelial cell size (polymegethism) is associated with long-term chronic hypoxia and acidosis from lens wear.

mcq.q: Diffuse punctate staining in both eyes after a new solution suggests
mcq.explanation: Diffuse punctate staining in both eyes soon after changing solution suggests solution toxicity or sensitivity.

mcq.q: What are mucin balls?
mcq.explanation: Mucin balls are small spheres of mucus and debris trapped under (usually stiffer) silicone hydrogel lenses. They leave pits that pool fluorescein.

mcq.q: A contact lens peripheral ulcer (CLPU) is usually
mcq.explanation: A CLPU is a small, round, peripheral, sterile infiltrate with overlying staining. It is usually less painful than microbial keratitis.

mcq.q: In marginal retro-illumination, epithelial microcysts show
mcq.explanation: Microcysts act as diverging lenses (higher index than the surrounding tissue), so in marginal retro-illumination they show reversed illumination.

mcq.q: Epithelial vacuoles show
mcq.explanation: Vacuoles are fluid-filled, with a lower index than the surroundings, so in retro-illumination they show unreversed illumination. This tells them apart from microcysts.

mcq.q: Endothelial blebs appear
mcq.explanation: Endothelial blebs appear within minutes of lens insertion in response to acute acidosis, and they settle after about 30 minutes.

mcq.q: Contact lens superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis is linked to
mcq.explanation: Contact lens SLK has been linked to hypersensitivity to preservatives such as thiomersal, along with mechanical irritation.

mcq.q: The 2006 Fusarium keratitis outbreak was linked to
mcq.explanation: The 2005–2006 Fusarium keratitis outbreak was linked to one multipurpose solution (ReNu with MoistureLoc), which was then withdrawn.

mcq.q: Pseudomonas keratitis typically

options.text: spreads fast, with discharge and a ring
resolves on its own in a few days
is painless and slow to progress
affects only the lids and lashes

mcq.explanation: Pseudomonas keratitis progresses quickly, with pain, discharge, a dense infiltrate and sometimes a ring infiltrate. It can perforate the cornea within days.

mcq.q: Suspected microbial keratitis should be managed by
mcq.explanation: Suspected microbial keratitis is an emergency: stop lens wear and refer the same day for corneal scrapes and intensive antibiotics. Don't patch the eye.

mcq.q: Why keep the lenses and case in suspected MK?
mcq.explanation: Lenses, the case and solution can be cultured to help identify the organism and guide treatment.

mcq.q: Which is the biggest risk factor for MK?
mcq.explanation: Overnight wear is the single biggest risk factor for contact lens microbial keratitis.

mcq.q: Corneal exhaustion syndrome is linked to

options.text: years of hypoxia from low-Dk lenses
a few weeks of lens wear

mcq.explanation: Corneal exhaustion syndrome is sudden intolerance to lenses after years of hypoxic (low-Dk) wear, with endothelial changes.

mcq.q: A corneal abrasion from a damaged lens shows
mcq.explanation: An abrasion from a damaged lens edge shows well-defined fluorescein staining that matches the shape of the damage.

mcq.q: Allergy to solution preservatives causes

options.text: an early cataract in both eyes

mcq.explanation: Preservative allergy causes red, itchy eyes in both eyes with diffuse punctate staining, and it improves when the solution is changed.

mcq.q: Infiltrative keratitis differs from MK because it's
mcq.explanation: Sterile infiltrative keratitis is usually small, peripheral and mild with little staining. MK is larger, more central, painful and ulcerated.

mcq.q: Corneal warpage from rigid lenses
mcq.explanation: Rigid lenses (especially PMMA or poorly fitting ones) can mould the cornea, changing its topography and refraction.

mcq.q: What's the usual first step for most lens complications?

options.text: Reduce or stop wear and review
Change to another brand without checking

mcq.explanation: Most lens complications start with reducing or stopping wear and reviewing, then fixing the cause (fit, material, hygiene, care system).

mcq.q: Which bacterium is Gram-positive?
mcq.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is Gram-positive. Pseudomonas, Serratia and E. coli are Gram-negative.

mcq.q: Which complication is a superficial epithelial lesion caused by a stiff lens under the upper lid?
mcq.explanation: A SEAL (superior epithelial arcuate lesion) is an arc-shaped lesion in the superior cornea caused by mechanical pressure from a stiff lens under the upper lid.

mcq.q: Contact lens papillary conjunctivitis is managed by
mcq.explanation: Stop or reduce wear to let the papillae settle (sometimes with mast cell stabilisers), then refit with more frequent replacement, ideally daily disposables.

mcq.q: Neovascularisation into the cornea mainly reflects
mcq.explanation: Corneal vessels grow in mainly because of chronic hypoxia from low-oxygen lenses or long wearing times.

mcq.q: A contact lens wearer with a white, staining lesion and severe pain should be treated as
mcq.explanation: A painful, white, staining lesion in a lens wearer should be treated as microbial keratitis and referred urgently until proven otherwise.

mcq.q: Which patient factor raises MK risk?
mcq.explanation: Smoking is a known independent risk factor for contact lens microbial keratitis.

mcq.q: How do you grade a corneal infiltrate's size?
mcq.explanation: Measure the infiltrate's size with the slit lamp graticule (or beam length) so it can be compared reliably over time.

mcq.q: Bacterial keratitis with a large infiltrate and hypopyon is
mcq.explanation: A large infiltrate with hypopyon shows severe bacterial keratitis. It is sight-threatening and needs emergency treatment.

mcq.q: A patient with recurrent CLPC wants to keep wearing soft lenses. Which change is most likely to help?
mcq.explanation: Deposits on reused lenses drive CLPC. A fresh daily lens has none, so dailies carry the lowest risk.

original.q: Which modality has the lowest risk of CLPC?

mcq.q: Which complication is an acute red eye on waking after overnight wear?
mcq.explanation: CLARE presents as an acute red, uncomfortable eye on waking after overnight lens wear.

mcq.q: Acanthamoeba keratitis is often first misdiagnosed as
mcq.explanation: Acanthamoeba keratitis can show a dendritic-like epitheliopathy, so it is often first misdiagnosed as herpes simplex keratitis, which delays the right treatment.

mcq.q: Why must symptoms be taken seriously in lens wearers?

options.text: So the practice can bill for it

mcq.explanation: Microbial keratitis, especially from Pseudomonas, can develop within hours, so any red, painful or blurred eye in a lens wearer needs prompt action.

mcq.q: Which test helps show epithelial damage in lens wearers?
mcq.explanation: Fluorescein staining shows epithelial damage, revealing abrasions, punctate staining and ulcers.

mcq.q: Why are smokers advised against overnight wear?
mcq.explanation: Smoking increases the risk of microbial keratitis, and combining it with overnight wear multiplies the risk.

cases.scenario: A 20-year-old who often naps in her monthly lenses presents with a red, painful right eye, photophobia and mucopurulent discharge. VA has dropped to 6/18. There's a 2.5 mm paracentral infiltrate that stains with fluorescein.
cases.question: What's your working diagnosis and management?
cases.modelAnswer: Presumed microbial keratitis (sleeping in lenses is a major risk factor). Remove lenses, don't let her reinsert them, keep the lenses and case for culture, and refer as an emergency (same day) to the hospital eye service. Explain why it's urgent. Record findings and advice.

cases.question: Describe the effects of contact lens wear on host defences, and give up to three toxic or allergic adverse events.
cases.modelAnswer: Host defences: Dk/t-dependent changes to corneal epithelial function; fewer PMNs; less sIgA. Toxic or allergic events: papillary conjunctivitis; solution-induced corneal staining; incompletely neutralised peroxide; limbal stem cell deficiency.

topics.askClaude: Describe 5 contact lens complications in a mixed-up order (signs and history only). Ask me to name each one and say how urgently to refer.

topics.title: Grading scales (Efron / CCLRU) and recording
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 6 lecture: grading anterior eye findings lets you monitor change, tell normal from abnormal and hand over care. Use a named scale, grade to 0.1, and know the strengths of photographic and painted scales and of digital imaging.
keyPoints: Five-point scale: 0 normal (no action), 1 trace (action rarely needed), 2 mild (possibly), 3 moderate (usually), 4 severe (required). Add + or −, and extrapolate to conditions not on the card.

Grade to 0.1: a one-grade change is clinically significant, and rounding hides real change (2.5 to 3.4 both become 3). Inter-observer variation can reach 55%; 50 optometrists grading one image gave 1.2 ± 0.5.

Photographic scales (e.g. CCLRU) are realistic but need a huge library and vary in magnification, angle and patient. Painted scales (e.g. Efron) are less realistic but show severity systematically. Morphing sequences didn't improve grading.
Grade bulbar and limbal redness, palpebral redness and roughness, and staining (CCLRU staining by area: under 15% to over 45%). Always name the scale.
Digital imaging records what words can't and allows measurement. Consider the camera (CCD or CMOS; one-chip or three-chip), slit lamp optics, illumination, storage and support.

Resolution: the smallest features (microcysts, punctate staining, about 30 µm) need a 2 × 2 pixel matrix. Objective grading uses edge detection and colour extraction (red ratio for redness, green for staining), e.g. Keratograph 5M redness scans.
examTraps: Not stating which scale you used.
Grading only in whole numbers.
Thinking a painted scale is less useful than a photo: it shows severity steps more systematically.

diagram.description: A row of five bulbar conjunctiva images labelled 0 to 4 with increasing redness, with words underneath: normal, trace, mild, moderate, severe. A bracket marks grades 3–4 as 'action'.

goDeeper.heading: Test-your-knowledge answers
goDeeper.body: Benefits of a grading scale: better record keeping, standardisation, monitoring, and patient communication. CCLRU is photographic; a painted scale's weakness is lack of realism.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: grading conditions
goDeeper.body: Grade under the same illumination and magnification each time, record both eyes, and note if drops were instilled or a lens had just been removed.

flashcards.back: 0 normal, 1 trace, 2 mild, 3 moderate, 4 severe.
Efron = painted illustrations; CCLRU (Brien Holden) = photographs.
About one grade.
Central, superior, inferior, nasal, temporal.
A real change (e.g. 2.5 to 3.4) can disappear if both are rounded to 3.

flashcards.front: Resolution needed for anterior eye imaging
flashcards.back: Enough for a 2 × 2 pixel matrix on the smallest features (about 30 µm: microcysts, punctate staining).

mcq.q: Limbal redness was graded 1.0 at the last aftercare and 2.2 today. What does this suggest?

options.feedback: Yes — over one grade of change.
A change of more than one grade is significant.
Grade 2 needs monitoring, and the change matters too.

options.text: A sign that lid eversion is needed
options.feedback: Not specifically indicated by limbal redness.

mcq.explanation: Grading to decimals lets you see trends. A rise of about one grade between visits deserves an explanation.

mcq.q: Which is a photographic grading scale?
mcq.explanation: The CCLRU (Brien Holden) scales use photographs. Efron's scales use paintings, which some find easier to match by eye.

mcq.q: Which statement about painted grading scales (e.g. Efron) is wrong?

options.text: They are more realistic than photographs
options.feedback: Yes, that's wrong: lack of realism is their main drawback.

options.text: They show one feature at a time

mcq.explanation: Painted scales are clear and consistent but less realistic than photographic scales.

original.q: Which is a disadvantage of a painted grading scale?

options.text: It is difficult to get different magnifications
Different patients have slightly different manifestations
options.feedback: That's a photographic scale problem; a painting can be idealised.

mcq.q: Limbal redness is graded 2.0 on a 0–4 scale. What does that usually mean?
mcq.explanation: 0 normal, 1 trace, 2 mild (action possibly), 3 moderate, 4 severe.

original.q: On a 0–4 scale, what does grade 2 usually mean?

mcq.q: Why grade to 0.1 rather than whole numbers?

options.text: Rounding hides real change between visits

mcq.explanation: Grading to 0.1 detects smaller changes between visits than whole numbers, which can hide real improvement or worsening.

mcq.q: What are photographic grading scales' main drawbacks?

options.text: Huge libraries; images vary a lot

mcq.explanation: Photographic scales need large image sets for each condition, and photos vary in lighting, magnification and field, which makes comparison harder.

mcq.q: A practice camera's pixels each cover 40 µm of the cornea. Can it reliably record punctate staining (about 30 µm)?
mcq.explanation: The smallest features (about 30 µm) need a resolution where each spans about 2 × 2 pixels.

original.q: What's the smallest feature size anterior eye images must resolve?

mcq.q: How do objective systems grade redness?

options.text: The red share of the image colour
With a ruler on the photo

mcq.explanation: Objective systems analyse a digital image, measuring the proportion of red (or vessel coverage) to give a redness score.

mcq.q: What must every graded record state?
mcq.explanation: Scales differ in their steps and anchors, so every grade must name the scale used for future comparisons to make sense.

mcq.q: Which is a widely used painted grading scale?
mcq.explanation: The Efron scales are painted artist's illustrations of contact lens complications at grades 0–4.

mcq.q: Which scale is photographic?
mcq.explanation: The CCLRU (Brien Holden Vision Institute) scales use photographs. The Efron scales are painted.

mcq.q: On a 0–4 scale, grade 3 means
mcq.explanation: On 0–4 scales: 0 is normal, 1 trace, 2 mild, 3 moderate and 4 severe.

mcq.q: Which change is usually clinically significant?
mcq.explanation: Changes within about 1 grade fall inside normal observer variability, so a change of more than one grade is usually clinically significant.

mcq.q: Clinical action is usually needed from about grade
mcq.explanation: Grades 0–2 usually need monitoring at most. From about grade 3 (moderate), clinical action is generally needed.

mcq.q: Why use the same scale each time?
mcq.explanation: Scales have different reference images and steps, so grades from different scales can't be compared directly.

mcq.q: What limits clinical grading?
mcq.explanation: Grading is subjective, so results vary between clinicians (inter-observer) and between repeat grades by the same clinician (intra-observer).

mcq.q: Why grade bulbar redness by zone?
mcq.explanation: Redness can vary between the nasal, temporal, superior, inferior and limbal zones, so grading each zone captures localised change.

mcq.q: What can capture images for grading?
mcq.explanation: A slit lamp with a camera captures images that can be graded and compared over time, either subjectively or objectively.

mcq.q: What is interpolation?
mcq.explanation: Interpolation means grading between the reference images (e.g. 1.5 or 2.3), which improves sensitivity to change.

mcq.q: On the Efron scale, grade 0 means
mcq.explanation: Efron grades run 0 (normal) to 4 (severe). Grades 0–1 usually need no action; 3–4 need it.

mcq.q: On the Efron scale, grade 1 means
mcq.explanation: Efron grade 1 is trace, which is usually not clinically significant.

mcq.q: On the Efron scale, grade 4 means
mcq.explanation: Efron grade 4 is severe, so you need to act, e.g. stop or change lens wear and treat or refer.

mcq.q: Corneal staining is often graded for
mcq.explanation: Corneal staining is graded for type (pattern), extent (area) and depth (how far fluorescein penetrates) in each zone.

mcq.q: Corneal staining is often recorded in how many zones?
mcq.explanation: Corneal staining is often recorded in five zones (central, superior, inferior, nasal, temporal), each graded separately.

mcq.q: Microcysts are usually graded by
mcq.explanation: Microcysts are graded by counting them in retro-illumination, which is more repeatable than a descriptive scale.

mcq.q: Which scheme grades staining in dry eye using panels A to E?
mcq.explanation: The Oxford scheme grades ocular surface staining using panels A to E (0–5) of increasing punctate density.

mcq.q: Agreement between two different clinicians grading the same eye is
mcq.explanation: Inter-observer reliability is the agreement between different clinicians grading the same eye.

mcq.q: Agreement when one clinician grades the same eye twice is
mcq.explanation: Intra-observer reliability is the agreement when the same clinician grades the same eye twice.

mcq.q: How can grading reliability be improved?
mcq.explanation: Training with standard reference images and using the same scale and method consistently improves reliability.

mcq.q: Why keep slit lamp settings consistent when grading?

options.text: For the colour of the image

mcq.explanation: Magnification, illumination and filters change how redness and staining look, so keep settings consistent so grades are comparable.

mcq.q: Which feature is graded in CLPC?
mcq.explanation: In CLPC, grade the papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva (size and redness) after everting the lid.

mcq.q: Why photograph findings as well as grading them?
mcq.explanation: Photos give a permanent record that can be compared directly at later visits or by other clinicians.

mcq.q: A grade drop from 3.0 to 1.5 after refitting suggests
mcq.explanation: A fall in grade from 3.0 to 1.5 suggests the condition has improved, for example after refitting.

mcq.q: Why should grading always state which eye and which scale?
mcq.explanation: Grades only make sense if the eye and scale are recorded, so someone else (or you later) can interpret and compare them.

mcq.q: Objective image analysis grades redness by
mcq.explanation: Image analysis software measures vessel coverage or the redness of the image, giving an objective, repeatable grade.

mcq.q: Which is graded as part of lid margin assessment?
mcq.explanation: Assessing the lid margin includes grading blepharitis and meibomian gland dysfunction, which affect lens comfort and complications.

mcq.q: Limbal redness is graded separately from bulbar redness because
mcq.explanation: Limbal redness is more specifically linked to hypoxia than general bulbar redness, so it is graded separately.

mcq.q: Which sign is often graded by how far it extends into the cornea?
mcq.explanation: Neovascularisation is graded by how far vessels extend past the limbus into the cornea (in mm) and by their extent.

mcq.q: Why is a description sometimes better than a grade?

options.text: Unusual signs may not fit a scale

mcq.explanation: Unusual or atypical signs may not match any scale image, so a clear written description (or a photo) records them better.

mcq.q: Grading scales help patients by
mcq.explanation: Grading consistently over time shows small worsening early, so problems can be managed before they become serious.

mcq.q: A learning effect in grading means
mcq.explanation: As clinicians gain experience, their grading can drift systematically. This is a learning effect that can affect comparisons over time.

mcq.q: Which redness level usually needs no action?
mcq.explanation: Grades 0–1 (normal to trace) usually need no action. Grade 2 needs monitoring, and grades 3–4 need action.

mcq.q: Grading conjunctival staining is useful for detecting

options.text: dry eye and lid wiper problems

mcq.explanation: Conjunctival staining, including lid wiper staining, helps detect dry eye and lid wiper epitheliopathy.

mcq.q: Which is graded with lissamine green?
mcq.explanation: Lissamine green stains dead and damaged cells and shows up well on the conjunctiva, so it is used to grade conjunctival staining.

mcq.q: When grading, why look at the same area each time?
mcq.explanation: Signs vary across the eye, so grade the same zones each time for valid comparisons.

mcq.q: The Efron scales cover about how many complications?
mcq.explanation: The Efron grading scales illustrate about 16 contact lens complications.

mcq.q: A redness grade is 2.0 in both eyes. What should you consider?

options.text: Compare with before; look for causes

mcq.explanation: Grade 2 is mild. Compare with previous visits and look for causes such as fit, material, hypoxia or dryness rather than acting automatically.

mcq.q: Which grading approach is most objective?
mcq.explanation: Computerised image analysis removes the observer's subjectivity, so it is the most objective and repeatable approach.

mcq.q: Grading in 0.5 steps rather than 0.1 is
mcq.explanation: Coarser 0.5 steps can miss small real changes that 0.1 steps would pick up.

cases.question: What are the key benefits of a clinical grading scale?
cases.modelAnswer: Better record keeping; standardisation between clinicians and visits; monitoring change over time; and clearer communication with patients (one mark each).

topics.askClaude: Describe some anterior eye findings in words and ask me to grade them on the Efron scale and say whether action is needed.

topics.title: Corneal shape and topography
topics.summary: The cornea is aspheric: steepest at the apex and flattening towards the limbus. Keratometry samples a small central zone; videokeratoscopy maps 7 to 9 mm, and the kind of map you choose changes what you can read from it.
keyPoints: Corneal radii range from about 7.4 to 8.8 mm. A 0.05 mm difference between meridians is about 0.25 D of corneal astigmatism.
Asphericity: e² = 1 − p = −Q. Circle e² = 0; prolate ellipse 0 to 1 (the normal cornea, mean about 0.22); parabola 1; hyperbola above 1; oblate below 0.
Colour maps: warm colours are steeper (shorter radius), cool colours flatter.
With-the-rule astigmatism gives a vertical bow tie; against-the-rule gives a horizontal bow tie.

Axial (sagittal) maps: most repeatable, but distort the position of the apex. Tangential (instantaneous) maps: best for locating the apex and local changes. Height maps: the most direct shape measure, used for refractive surgery and simulated fluorescein patterns.
Topography shows things keratometry misses: irregular and asymmetric astigmatism, keratoconus, and orthokeratology treatment zones.
examTraps: Comparing two maps without checking the scale. Relative and absolute scales colour the same cornea differently.
Assuming topography measures the cornea directly. Placido systems read the tear film, so a poor tear film breaks up the rings.
Forgetting that a 2.5 mm decentration can create about 1 D of false astigmatism: alignment matters.

goDeeper.heading: Where videokeratoscopy goes wrong
goDeeper.body: Sources of error listed in the lecture: paraxial assumptions that are poor in the periphery, the image coming from the tear film, poor fixation, image quality, focusing, the same number of points being analysed per ring (area sampling bias), bowl size, number of rings, and alignment. Accuracy is best for the intermediate rings.

goDeeper.heading: Alignment
goDeeper.body: Ideally a map would be centred on the line of sight through the entrance pupil. The instrument instead lines up perpendicular to the cornea, towards its centre of curvature, so the map centre is often not the pupil centre.

flashcards.back: Greater than 1.

flashcards.front: Relationship between e, p and Q
flashcards.back: e² = 1 − p = −Q.
Horizontal. (With-the-rule is vertical.)

flashcards.front: Which map is best for finding the corneal apex?
flashcards.back: Tangential (instantaneous). Axial maps distort its position.

mcq.q: In a hyperbola, e² is

options.feedback: That is a prolate ellipse, like the normal cornea.

mcq.explanation: For a hyperbola, e² is greater than 1.

mcq.q: A topography map shows a symmetric red bow tie running horizontally. What does it mean?

options.feedback: Yes: the horizontal meridian is steeper.

mcq.explanation: With-the-rule gives a vertical bow tie; against-the-rule gives a horizontal one.

original.q: In against-the-rule astigmatism, the corneal topography map looks like

options.feedback: Yes. The steep meridian is horizontal, so the warm colours lie horizontally.
That is with-the-rule: the lecture notes that red lies vertically in with-the-rule astigmatism.

options.text: a vertical bow tie with a horizontal bow tie against it
options.feedback: Regular astigmatism gives a single bow tie along the steep meridian.

original.explanation: Test-your-knowledge question 4. Answer worked out from the lecture: the bow tie follows the steep meridian.

mcq.q: What shape is the normal cornea?
mcq.explanation: The normal cornea is a prolate ellipse: steepest at the centre and flattening towards the periphery.

mcq.q: What's the average corneal e?
mcq.explanation: The average corneal eccentricity is about 0.47 (e² ≈ 0.22). 0 is a sphere and 1 is a parabola.

mcq.q: With-the-rule astigmatism shows which bow tie on a map?
mcq.explanation: In WTR astigmatism the vertical meridian is steeper, so the steep (warm-coloured) bow tie runs vertically on the map.

mcq.q: Warm colours on a topography map mean
mcq.explanation: On curvature maps, warm colours (red, orange) show steeper areas and cool colours (blue) show flatter areas.

mcq.q: You want to compare maps from two visits to check for subtle change. Which map type gives the most repeatable readings?

options.feedback: Better for local shape, less repeatable.

mcq.explanation: Axial maps are most repeatable; tangential maps show local shape better.

original.q: Which map is most repeatable?

options.feedback: Yes, but it distorts the apex position.
Better for the apex but less repeatable.

mcq.q: Which map best suits refractive surgery planning and simulated fluorescein patterns?
mcq.explanation: Elevation (height) maps show the cornea's shape against a reference surface. This is what refractive surgery and simulated rigid lens fluorescein patterns need.

mcq.q: About how much false astigmatism can 2.5 mm of misalignment create?
mcq.explanation: Misaligning the topographer by around 2.5 mm can create about 1 D of false astigmatism, so centring and alignment are critical.

mcq.q: What area does videokeratoscopy typically cover?
mcq.explanation: Placido-based videokeratoscopes typically cover about 7–9 mm of the cornea, far more than the central 3 mm a keratometer measures.

mcq.q: Which principle does a Placido disc topographer use?
mcq.explanation: A Placido topographer projects concentric illuminated rings onto the cornea and analyses their reflected image. The spacing of the rings shows the local curvature.

mcq.q: Which system measures both corneal surfaces?
mcq.explanation: Scheimpflug imaging photographs optical sections of the cornea, so it can map front and back elevation as well as thickness. Placido systems only measure the front.

mcq.q: You suspect a small inferior cone. Which map shows its local shape best?
mcq.explanation: Tangential maps show local curvature changes such as a cone.

original.q: Which map best shows local shape such as a cone?

mcq.q: Keratoconus typically shows
mcq.explanation: Keratoconus typically shows focal steepening below the centre, giving inferior–superior asymmetry, often with an asymmetric or skewed bow tie.

mcq.q: e = 0 describes a
mcq.explanation: Eccentricity 0 is a sphere, between 0 and 1 is a prolate ellipse, 1 is a parabola, and above 1 is a hyperbola.

mcq.q: If e = 0.45, what's p?
An elevation map shows height relative to
mcq.explanation: Elevation maps show the corneal height above or below a reference surface, usually a best-fit sphere.

mcq.q: After orthokeratology, the map shows
mcq.explanation: Ortho-k flattens the central cornea, and the mid-periphery steepens around it, giving a centred 'bull's eye': a cool centre with a warm ring.

mcq.q: Why use an absolute scale?
mcq.explanation: An absolute scale uses the same fixed colour steps on every map, so maps from different visits or patients can be compared directly.

mcq.q: An asymmetric bow tie suggests
mcq.explanation: A regular cornea shows a symmetric bow tie. An asymmetric or skewed bow tie suggests irregular astigmatism, for example early keratoconus.

mcq.q: Closely spaced Placido rings indicate a
mcq.explanation: Steeper areas reflect a smaller mire image, so the Placido rings appear closer together. Wider spacing means flatter areas.

mcq.q: An axial (sagittal) map
mcq.explanation: Axial (sagittal) maps measure curvature relative to the instrument axis. This smooths local changes, while tangential maps show local steepening better.

mcq.q: A normalised colour scale

options.text: adapts its range to each map

mcq.explanation: A normalised scale sets its colour range from each map's own minimum and maximum, so the steps change from map to map.

mcq.q: Why can normalised scales mislead?
mcq.explanation: With a normalised scale, even small differences in power are spread across the full colour range. A nearly normal cornea can look dramatically abnormal.

mcq.q: Simulated K (Sim K) values come from
mcq.explanation: Sim K values are the topographer's estimate of the central principal meridian powers over the zone a keratometer would measure.

mcq.q: Inferior steepening greater than superior is a sign of
mcq.explanation: Inferior steepening greater than superior steepening (a raised I–S value) is a key topographic sign of keratoconus.

mcq.q: A 'crab-claw' or 'kissing birds' pattern suggests
mcq.explanation: Pellucid marginal degeneration gives a 'crab-claw' or 'kissing birds' pattern: steepening in the inferior periphery with flattening along the vertical axis.

mcq.q: An ortho-k lens that rides low shows a
mcq.explanation: If the ortho-k lens rides low, the treatment zone decentres downwards. This gives a 'smiley face' arc of steepening above it rather than a centred ring.

mcq.q: After myopic LASIK, the topography shows
mcq.explanation: Myopic LASIK removes central stromal tissue, so the central cornea flattens.

mcq.q: Rigid lens warpage on topography looks

options.text: irregular, flat where the lens sat
like a bow tie and nothing else

mcq.explanation: Rigid lens warpage gives irregular topography, often flattened where the lens sat and steeper elsewhere.

mcq.q: Scheimpflug devices can map
mcq.explanation: Scheimpflug devices build a 3D model of the cornea, so they can produce thickness (pachymetry) maps, including the thinnest point.

mcq.q: Why does a poor tear film affect Placido topography?
mcq.explanation: Placido systems image the rings reflected by the tear film, so dry patches or an irregular tear film distort the rings and give false readings.

mcq.q: Which instrument measures corneal epithelial thickness?
mcq.explanation: Anterior segment OCT resolves the corneal layers and can map epithelial thickness.

mcq.q: Corneal eccentricity is especially useful in
mcq.explanation: Eccentricity describes how the cornea flattens towards the periphery, which matters when choosing rigid and ortho-k back surface designs.

mcq.q: A regular symmetric bow tie suggests
mcq.explanation: A symmetric bow tie with the halves aligned along one meridian is the typical pattern of regular astigmatism.

mcq.q: Warm colours on a power map show
mcq.explanation: On power and curvature maps, warm colours (red, orange) show steeper, more powerful areas.

mcq.q: Cool colours on a power map show
mcq.explanation: On power and curvature maps, cool colours (blue) show flatter, less powerful areas.

mcq.q: A refractive power map uses
mcq.explanation: Refractive power maps use Snell's law at the corneal surface to calculate the true refractive power at each point.

mcq.q: Why monitor keratoconus with topography?
mcq.explanation: Repeat topography detects increasing steepening early, so cross-linking can be offered before vision is lost.

mcq.q: Corneal cross-linking aims to

options.text: stiffen the cornea and halt ectasia

mcq.explanation: Corneal cross-linking uses riboflavin and UVA to create extra collagen bonds, stiffening the cornea and halting progressive ectasia such as keratoconus.

mcq.q: An elevation map's red area above the best-fit sphere shows
mcq.explanation: On elevation maps, warm colours mark points above the best-fit reference surface and cool colours mark points below it.

mcq.q: Posterior elevation maps help detect
mcq.explanation: Changes in the back surface can appear before front surface changes, so posterior elevation maps help detect early or subclinical keratoconus.

mcq.q: What's a key limitation of Placido topography?
mcq.explanation: Placido topographers only measure the front corneal surface, and they depend on a good tear film.

mcq.q: Why must the patient fixate centrally during topography?
mcq.explanation: If the patient doesn't fixate centrally, the map is decentred and can show false asymmetry or astigmatism.

mcq.q: How does a normal cornea change from centre to periphery?
mcq.explanation: A normal cornea is prolate: steepest centrally and flattening gradually towards the periphery.

mcq.q: Which is a topography-based keratoconus screening approach?
mcq.explanation: The I–S index compares inferior with superior corneal power. A raised value is a common topographic screen for keratoconus.

mcq.q: A 'bull's eye' after ortho-k means
mcq.explanation: A centred bull's eye (central flattening ringed by steepening) shows a well-centred ortho-k treatment zone.

mcq.q: Topography can help explain
mcq.explanation: Topography can reveal irregular astigmatism, ectasia or warpage that explains unexplained astigmatism or reduced acuity.

mcq.q: Which map is best for comparing two visits?
mcq.explanation: A difference map subtracts one map from another, showing exactly where and how much the cornea changed between visits.

mcq.q: Videokeratoscopes measure height or curvature at
mcq.explanation: Videokeratoscopes analyse thousands of points across the cornea, while a keratometer only gives two meridian readings.

cases.scenario: A 19-year-old's astigmatism has increased at each of the last three visits and best corrected acuity is now 6/9. Topography shows inferior steepening and retinoscopy gives a scissoring reflex.
cases.question: What do you suspect and what do you do?
cases.modelAnswer: Keratoconus: progressive irregular astigmatism in a young patient, inferior steepening on topography, a scissor reflex and reduced best corrected acuity. Look on the slit lamp for corneal thinning, Vogt's striae and a Fleischer ring, and ask about eye rubbing and atopy. Refer to ophthalmology promptly, because corneal collagen cross-linking can halt progression if it is done while the disease is still progressing. Advise against eye rubbing. Vision is usually best with rigid or specialist contact lenses once irregularity is significant.
