topics.title: Tear film and contact lenses
topics.summary: A contact lens splits the tear film and depends on it for comfort, wetting and oxygen. Know where each layer comes from, what changes it, and how to measure tear quantity, quality and stability before and during lens wear.
keyPoints: Lipid: meibomian glands and glands of Zeis and Moll; 0.1–0.2 µm; reduces evaporation; seen as interference fringes.
Aqueous: main lacrimal gland (reflex) and accessory glands of Krause and Wolfring (basal); about 7 µm; carries ions, glucose, proteins (lysozyme, lactoferrin, lipocalin, IgA) and vitamin A.
Mucin: conjunctival goblet cells and corneal epithelium; makes the surface wettable and stops bacteria adhering.
Volume about 7 µl, made at about 1.2 µl/min, turned over every 5 minutes; open-eye osmolarity about 315 mOsm/kg.
Blink rate about 12/min, reduced by reading, hard tasks and screens; partial blinks cause 3 and 9 o'clock staining with rigid lenses.
Tests: quantity (Schirmer, phenol red thread, meniscus height), stability (TBUT, NIBUT), lipid (Tearscope), damage (fluorescein, rose bengal, lissamine green) and symptoms (OSDI).
examTraps: Calling TBUT a test of tear secretion: it measures stability. Schirmer and phenol red measure quantity.
Thinking fluorescein TBUT is non-invasive: the drop adds volume to the tear film. NIBUT avoids that.

goDeeper.heading: Proteins and lenses
goDeeper.body: Lysozyme is small and strongly positively charged, so it's drawn into negatively charged (ionic, methacrylic acid) hydrogel lenses. When proteins attach to a hydrophobic surface their 3D structure unfolds (denatures), which can trigger discomfort and inflammation.

flashcards.front: Three dyes for ocular surface staining
flashcards.back: Sodium fluorescein, rose bengal, lissamine green.
The main lacrimal gland (reflex) and the accessory glands of Krause and Wolfring (basal).
Reading, harder tasks, computer use, corneal anaesthesia.
About 7 µl, made at about 1.2 µl/min, fully turned over about every 5 minutes.

mcq.q: Which is a source of the tear film's lipid layer?

options.feedback: Yes, with the meibomian glands and glands of Zeis.

mcq.explanation: The glands of Moll, Zeis and the meibomian glands all contribute lipid.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a test of tear secretion?
mcq.explanation: Tear break-up time measures tear film stability, not secretion.

mcq.q: A patient has blocked meibomian glands and inflamed lash follicles. Which tear layer is most at risk?

options.feedback: Yes: from meibomian glands and glands of Zeis and Moll.

mcq.explanation: The lipid layer comes from the meibomian glands and the glands of Zeis and Moll.

original.q: Which glands produce the lipid layer?

options.text: Meibomian glands and glands of Zeis and Moll

mcq.q: Which layer makes up most of the tear film's thickness?
mcq.explanation: The aqueous layer is about 7 µm, far thicker than the lipid layer.

original.q: About how thick is the aqueous layer?

mcq.q: Tear volume is about 7 µl and production about 1.2 µl per minute. Roughly how long does the tear volume take to turn over?
mcq.explanation: Tear volume is about 7 µl, turned over roughly every 5 minutes.

original.q: Tear volume is about

mcq.q: Which test measures tear stability?
mcq.explanation: Tear break-up time (with fluorescein, or non-invasive NIBUT) measures how long the tear film stays stable after a blink. Schirmer and phenol red measure quantity.

mcq.q: A rigid lens wearer has staining at the 3 and 9 o'clock positions. What's a common cause?
mcq.explanation: Partial blinks with rigid lenses typically cause 3 and 9 o'clock staining.

original.q: Partial blinking with rigid lenses typically causes

mcq.q: What does lysozyme do?

options.text: Kills bacteria; drawn to ionic lenses

mcq.explanation: Lysozyme is an antibacterial enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls. Its positive charge draws it to negatively charged ionic lens materials.

mcq.q: Which reduces blink rate?

options.feedback: Yes, as do reading and hard tasks.

mcq.explanation: Concentrating on computer screens, reading or other demanding tasks lowers the blink rate, which increases evaporation and dryness.

mcq.q: A patient with conjunctival scarring loses goblet cells. What happens to the tear film?
mcq.explanation: Conjunctival goblet cells make the mucin that lets the tear film spread over the eye's surface. Lose them, from scarring or chemical injury, and the film won't wet the eye properly.

original.q: Which cells produce the mucin layer?

mcq.q: Which statement about aqueous tear production is wrong?

options.text: Accessory lacrimal glands only produce reflex tears
options.feedback: Yes, that's wrong: they contribute basal tears.

options.text: The main lacrimal gland drives reflex tearing
Krause and Wolfring glands are accessory glands
Basal and reflex tears both contribute

mcq.explanation: The main lacrimal gland gives reflex tears; the accessory glands of Krause and Wolfring give basal tears.

original.q: Which glands contribute to the aqueous layer?

options.text: The main and accessory (Krause, Wolfring) lacrimal glands

mcq.q: How long is the phenol red thread test?
mcq.explanation: The phenol red thread test takes 15 seconds. The thread turns red as it absorbs tears, and the length that changes colour is measured.

mcq.q: A normal Schirmer I (no anaesthetic) result in 5 minutes is
mcq.explanation: Schirmer I without anaesthetic: wetting of more than 10 mm in 5 minutes is normal, and 5 mm or less suggests aqueous deficiency.

mcq.q: A normal blink rate is about
mcq.explanation: A normal spontaneous blink rate is about 15–20 blinks per minute, and it falls during concentrated tasks.

mcq.q: What does lactoferrin do?

options.text: It's part of the lipid layer

mcq.explanation: Lactoferrin binds iron, which bacteria need to grow, so it acts as an antibacterial tear protein.

mcq.q: The pre-lens tear film
mcq.explanation: The tear film in front of a lens is thinner and less stable than over the cornea, so it breaks up and evaporates faster.

mcq.q: A normal tear meniscus height is about
mcq.explanation: A lower tear meniscus height of about 0.2 mm or more is normal. Lower values suggest aqueous deficiency.

mcq.q: Lid wiper epitheliopathy is best seen with
mcq.explanation: Lid wiper epitheliopathy is staining of the marginal conjunctiva of the upper lid, best seen with lissamine green (or fluorescein).

mcq.q: Why can lenses worsen dry eye symptoms?

options.text: They split the film, raising evaporation
They add extra tears to the eye
They don't affect dry eye at all
They block the puncta from draining

mcq.explanation: A lens splits the tear film into thinner pre-lens and post-lens layers. The pre-lens film breaks up and evaporates faster, which worsens dryness.

mcq.q: Which mucin is secreted by goblet cells?
mcq.explanation: MUC5AC is the main gel-forming mucin secreted by conjunctival goblet cells. MUC1, MUC4 and MUC16 are membrane-bound.

mcq.q: The glycocalyx is formed by
mcq.explanation: Membrane-bound mucins (MUC1, MUC4, MUC16) on the epithelial surface form the glycocalyx, which makes the surface wettable.

mcq.q: Which is the main immunoglobulin in tears?
mcq.explanation: Secretory IgA is the main immunoglobulin in tears, giving immune defence at the mucosal surface.

mcq.q: Normal tear pH is about
mcq.explanation: Normal tear pH is about 7.4, close to neutral, though it varies slightly through the day.

mcq.q: Normal tear osmolarity is about
mcq.explanation: Normal tear osmolarity is about 300 mOsm/L. Values above about 308 suggest dry eye.

mcq.q: Tears drain through the
mcq.explanation: Tears drain through the upper and lower puncta, along the canaliculi into the lacrimal sac, then down the nasolacrimal duct.

mcq.q: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the
mcq.explanation: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus of the nose, under the inferior turbinate.

mcq.q: Basal tear production is roughly
mcq.explanation: Basal tear production is about 1–1.5 µL per minute. Reflex tearing can increase it greatly.

mcq.q: Reflex tearing's afferent pathway is
mcq.explanation: Sensory input for reflex tearing comes from the cornea and conjunctiva through the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

mcq.q: Reflex tearing's efferent (parasympathetic) pathway travels with
mcq.explanation: Parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland travel with the facial nerve (CN VII), via the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion.

mcq.q: Most of the tear volume sits in the
mcq.explanation: Most of the tear volume (around 75–90%) sits in the upper and lower tear menisci. Only a small amount spreads over the cornea.

mcq.q: Which interferometry pattern suggests a thin lipid layer?
mcq.explanation: On interferometry, an open meshwork pattern means a thin lipid layer. Amorphous and coloured fringe patterns mean thicker layers.

mcq.q: Coloured interference fringes suggest
mcq.explanation: Coloured interference fringes show a thick lipid layer, which can occur with meibomian gland changes.

mcq.q: Schirmer II involves
mcq.explanation: Schirmer II measures reflex tearing by irritating the nasal mucosa (with a cotton bud) while the strip is in place.

mcq.q: Tear exchange under a soft lens with each blink is about
mcq.explanation: Soft lenses cover the cornea and conjunctiva, so only about 1–2% of the tears under the lens are exchanged with each blink. Debris can build up underneath.

mcq.q: Tear exchange under a rigid lens with each blink is about
mcq.explanation: Smaller rigid lenses move more and have edge lift, so about 10–20% of the post-lens tears are exchanged with each blink.

mcq.q: Lipocalin in tears

options.text: is one of the main mucins

mcq.explanation: Lipocalin binds lipids and helps stabilise the tear film by reducing surface tension.

mcq.q: Which device measures NIBUT automatically?
mcq.explanation: Keratograph-type systems project a Placido or grid pattern and automatically detect when it distorts, giving an objective NIBUT.

mcq.q: The TFOS DEWS II definition of dry eye includes

options.text: a low Schirmer and nothing else

mcq.explanation: TFOS DEWS II defines dry eye as a multifactorial disease with loss of tear film homeostasis and ocular symptoms, involving tear instability, hyperosmolarity, inflammation and damage.

mcq.q: Why does lens wear thin the pre-lens tear film?
mcq.explanation: The lens splits the tear film, leaving a thin pre-lens layer that breaks up and evaporates faster.

mcq.q: The post-lens tear film under a soft lens is

options.text: the same as the pre-lens film

mcq.explanation: The post-lens tear film under a soft lens is very thin, only a few micrometres, which limits tear exchange.

mcq.q: Which protein is antibacterial and breaks bacterial cell walls?
mcq.explanation: Lysozyme is an antibacterial enzyme that breaks bonds in bacterial cell walls.

mcq.q: Rose bengal stains

options.text: cells without mucin, and dead cells

mcq.explanation: Rose bengal stains cells not protected by mucin, as well as dead or damaged cells.

mcq.q: Why does rose bengal sting more than lissamine?
mcq.explanation: Rose bengal is toxic to epithelial cells, so it stings much more than lissamine green.

mcq.q: Which eyelid structure spreads the tear film on blinking?
mcq.explanation: The lid wiper, the part of the upper lid margin that touches the eye, spreads the tear film across the surface with each blink.

mcq.q: Which test suits measuring lipid layer quality?
mcq.explanation: Interferometry shows the patterns of the tear lipid layer, which indicate its thickness and quality.

mcq.q: What's a symptom questionnaire specific to lens wearers?
mcq.explanation: The CLDEQ-8 is an 8-item questionnaire designed for dryness and discomfort in contact lens wearers.

mcq.q: A patient's NIBUT is 4 seconds. What does it suggest?
mcq.explanation: A NIBUT under about 10 seconds suggests poor tear stability, and 4 seconds is clearly reduced.

mcq.q: Blinking also helps
mcq.explanation: Blinking spreads the tears and also pumps them through the puncta into the drainage system.

mcq.q: Which hormone change is linked with more dry eye?
mcq.explanation: Falling androgen levels around the menopause are linked to meibomian gland dysfunction and more dry eye.

cases.question: List the range of clinical dry eye tests and what each measures.
cases.modelAnswer: Quality and stability: NIBUT, TBUT and meniscus regularity [2]. Quantity: phenol red thread and Schirmer [2]. Lipid layer: Tearscope [2]. Surface damage: corneal and conjunctival staining [2]. Symptoms: OSDI questionnaire [2]. Bonus: osmolarity (TearLab) [1].

topics.title: Contact lens modalities, market and optics
topics.summary: How often lenses are replaced, why disposables became standard, why people stop wearing lenses, and the optical differences between contact lenses and spectacles.
keyPoints: Modalities: conventional (worn until worn out), planned or frequent replacement, and disposables (from 1987).

Disposables: fewer deposit problems (papillary conjunctivitis, red eyes, poor comfort and VA), fewer unscheduled visits, higher-water lenses possible, spares, simpler care, better management and more patient contact.
UK: about 4.75 million wearers, Europe's largest market. 20–50% of wearers drop out, half because of discomfort.
Wettability: sessile drop, Wilhelmy plate, captive bubble (in vitro); tear break-up (in vivo).
Measure contact lens BVP with a small focimeter stop; vertex distance correction Fcl = Fsp ÷ (1 − dFsp).
Myopes accommodate more in contact lenses than in spectacles (so may need a reading add sooner); hyperopes accommodate less.
Extended wear: up to 6 nights and 7 days; continuous wear: up to 30 nights. Any corneal compromise means daily wear only.
Daily versus extended wear decisions: corneal status, risk factors, Rx, tear film, lid integrity, environment, individual characteristics.
examTraps: Listing EOP as a wettability test: it measures oxygen at the cornea.
Forgetting solution costs and chair time when comparing the cost of modalities.

flashcards.front: Main reason people stop wearing contact lenses
flashcards.back: Discomfort (about half of drop-outs).
Fcl = Fsp ÷ (1 − d × Fsp), with d in metres.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a contact lens wettability measurement?

options.feedback: Yes: equivalent oxygen percentage measures oxygen under the lens.

mcq.explanation: Equivalent oxygen percentage measures oxygen under the lens.

mcq.q: In which case is accommodative demand lower with contact lenses than with spectacles?

options.feedback: Yes: so presbyopic symptoms may be postponed.
Myopes accommodate more with contact lenses.
Depends on the type of error.

mcq.explanation: Hypermetropes need less accommodation with contact lenses than with spectacles, so presbyopic symptoms may come later.

mcq.q: Based on 2024 data, the estimated US contact lens market revenue is

options.feedback: That's close to the global, not US, figure.

mcq.explanation: Estimated US contact lens market revenue for 2024 is over US$6 billion (about US$6.08 bn).

mcq.q: A patient sleeps in hydrogel lenses from Monday morning to Sunday morning, removing them for one night a week. Which wear pattern is this?
mcq.explanation: Extended wear means up to 6 nights and 7 days; continuous wear up to 30 nights.

original.q: Extended wear means wearing lenses for up to

options.feedback: Yes; continuous wear is up to 30 nights.

mcq.q: A cornea shows microcysts and limbal vascularisation. Which modality should you offer?

options.feedback: Yes: signs of compromise rule out extended wear.

mcq.explanation: Microcysts and limbal vascularisation show the cornea is already hypoxically compromised, so only daily wear (ideally high-Dk) should be offered.

mcq.q: Which statement about UK contact lens wear is wrong?

options.text: Almost nobody stops wearing lenses once they start
options.feedback: Yes, that's wrong: 20–50% drop out, often from discomfort.

options.text: The UK is one of Europe's largest markets
Discomfort is a common reason to stop

mcq.explanation: The UK has about 4.75 million wearers, and many people drop out, often because of discomfort.

original.q: About how many UK contact lens wearers are there?

mcq.q: Which costs least to the patient?

options.text: It depends on use and care costs

mcq.explanation: Total cost depends on how often the patient wears lenses and on care solution costs, so the cheapest option varies.

mcq.q: Name a non-optical reason for choosing a replacement schedule.

options.feedback: Yes; also cost, convenience and stock.

mcq.explanation: Replacement schedules are also chosen for non-optical reasons such as therapeutic use, cost, convenience and parameter availability.

mcq.q: Which modality needs no solutions or case?
mcq.explanation: Daily disposables are thrown away after each use, so no case or solutions are needed.

mcq.q: Continuous wear with silicone hydrogels can be up to
mcq.explanation: Some silicone hydrogels are approved for continuous wear of up to 30 nights.

mcq.q: What is orthokeratology?

options.text: Overnight lenses that reshape the cornea
A form of laser eye surgery

mcq.explanation: Orthokeratology uses reverse-geometry rigid lenses worn overnight to flatten the central cornea temporarily, so the wearer sees clearly without lenses during the day.

mcq.q: What's monovision?

options.text: One eye for distance, one for near
Only one eye corrected at all

mcq.explanation: Monovision corrects one eye (usually the dominant one) for distance and the other for near, to manage presbyopia.

mcq.q: Which lens suits a very irregular cornea?
mcq.explanation: Scleral lenses vault the irregular cornea and rest on the sclera, with a smooth saline-filled optical surface. This gives good vision on very irregular corneas.

mcq.q: What is a hybrid lens?

options.text: A rigid centre with a soft skirt

mcq.explanation: A hybrid lens has a rigid gas permeable centre for sharp optics and a soft skirt for comfort and centration.

mcq.q: Centre-near and centre-distance designs are types of
mcq.explanation: Centre-near and centre-distance designs are simultaneous-vision multifocal contact lenses.

mcq.q: Conventional soft lenses are replaced about
mcq.explanation: Conventional (traditional) soft lenses are reusable and replaced about once a year.

mcq.q: Why might a daily disposable be best for an occasional wearer?

options.text: Fresh lenses, no care, lower cost

mcq.explanation: For occasional wear, dailies give a fresh sterile lens each time, need no care routine and are only paid for when used.

mcq.q: Opaque tints are used to
mcq.explanation: Opaque tints cover the iris pattern to change eye colour, or to mask a disfigured eye.

mcq.q: Flexible wear means
mcq.explanation: Flexible wear means daily wear with occasional overnight wear, such as one night now and then.

mcq.q: Extended wear with soft lenses traditionally means up to
mcq.explanation: Extended wear traditionally means up to 6 nights (7 days) of continuous wear, then a night off. Continuous wear means up to 30 nights.

mcq.q: Mini-scleral lenses are about
mcq.explanation: Mini-scleral lenses are about 15–18 mm across. Larger sclerals go above about 18 mm.

mcq.q: Scleral lenses are filled with
mcq.explanation: The bowl of a scleral lens is filled with sterile, preservative-free saline before insertion, giving a fluid reservoir over the cornea.

mcq.q: Which patients benefit from scleral lenses for comfort?
mcq.explanation: Scleral lenses keep the cornea bathed in fluid, which helps severe ocular surface disease such as Sjögren's or graft-versus-host disease.

mcq.q: A piggyback system is

options.text: a rigid lens over a soft lens
a hybrid lens with a soft skirt

mcq.explanation: In a piggyback system, a rigid lens sits on top of a soft lens. The rigid lens gives the optics and the soft lens gives comfort and protection.

mcq.q: PMMA has a Dk of about
mcq.explanation: PMMA is essentially impermeable to oxygen (Dk ≈ 0), which is why gas permeable materials replaced it.

mcq.q: An enhancement tint is
mcq.explanation: Enhancement tints are translucent. They intensify or alter light-coloured irises without hiding the iris pattern.

mcq.q: Why are novelty (Halloween) lenses risky?
mcq.explanation: Novelty lenses are often sold without fitting or aftercare and may be poorly made, which is linked to serious infections. In the UK they must still be supplied under supervision.

mcq.q: Which modality may reduce plastic waste per year?
mcq.explanation: Reusable monthly or rigid lenses produce less packaging and plastic waste per year than daily disposables.

mcq.q: For a patient with high astigmatism who wants dailies, which option might exist?
mcq.explanation: Daily disposable toric lenses are available for many astigmatic prescriptions.

mcq.q: Which lens type is best for keratoconus with poor rigid comfort?
mcq.explanation: Scleral or hybrid lenses vault the cone or add a soft skirt for comfort, while still giving the sharp optics of a rigid surface.

mcq.q: Why do many practitioners favour silicone hydrogels for full-time wear?
mcq.explanation: Silicone hydrogels' high Dk greatly reduces hypoxic complications such as neovascularisation and microcysts in full-time wear.

mcq.q: Which modality has the best compliance with replacement?
mcq.explanation: With dailies, every lens is thrown away after one use, so wearers comply with replacement best. Monthly lenses are often over-worn.

mcq.q: A quarterly lens is replaced every
mcq.explanation: Quarterly lenses are replaced every 3 months: a middle ground between monthlies and yearly (conventional) lenses.

mcq.q: What does multifocal CL 'simultaneous vision' mean?

options.text: Both images are on the retina at once
The lens moves between its zones
Each eye is set for one distance
There's no near zone in the lens

mcq.explanation: Simultaneous-vision multifocals put the distance and near images on the retina at the same time, and the brain picks out the one in focus.

mcq.q: Translating (alternating) rigid bifocals work by
mcq.explanation: Translating rigid bifocals are pushed up by the lower lid on down-gaze, so the pupil moves from the distance zone into the near zone.

mcq.q: Which modality is often recommended for children starting lenses?
mcq.explanation: Dailies are often recommended for children because they need no care routine and lower the risk of complications.

mcq.q: A key advantage of rigid lenses is
mcq.explanation: Rigid lenses give sharp optics and correct corneal astigmatism through the tear lens.

mcq.q: A key disadvantage of rigid lenses is

options.text: they can't be used for keratoconus

mcq.explanation: Rigid lenses cause noticeable lid awareness at first, so they need a period of adaptation.

mcq.q: Myopia control soft lenses work by
mcq.explanation: Myopia control lenses keep central vision clear while adding peripheral myopic defocus, which is thought to slow axial elongation.

mcq.q: Which is a reason to choose a monthly over a daily?

options.text: Lower cost or a special parameter

mcq.explanation: Monthlies can be cheaper for full-time wearers, and they come in a wider range of special parameters (e.g. high toric powers).

mcq.q: Which modality is used for drug delivery research?
mcq.explanation: Drug-eluting contact lenses are being developed (and some are approved) to release medication onto the eye over time.

mcq.q: Corneoscleral lenses are about
mcq.explanation: Corneoscleral lenses (about 12.5–15 mm) land at the limbus area, between corneal rigid lenses and sclerals.

mcq.q: Which modality is linked with the most CLPC?
mcq.explanation: Deposits build up on infrequently replaced lenses, and these are strongly linked to CLPC.

mcq.q: Which factor matters most in choosing a modality?

options.text: Wear pattern, eye health, care ability
The design of the lens box
The colour of the lens tint

mcq.explanation: The best modality depends on how often the patient wears lenses, their ocular health and their ability to comply with care.

mcq.q: What do UV-blocking contact lenses not protect?
mcq.explanation: UV-blocking lenses only cover the cornea, so the conjunctiva, lids and surrounding skin still need sunglasses or a hat.

mcq.q: A rigid gas permeable lens of high Dk is suitable for

options.text: daily wear, and some extended wear

mcq.explanation: High-Dk rigid lenses give plenty of oxygen for daily wear, and some are approved for extended wear.

mcq.q: What is a 'reverse geometry' lens?

options.text: A rigid ortho-k lens, flat centre, steep ring
A soft lens worn inside out
A type of spectacle lens design

mcq.explanation: Ortho-k lenses use reverse geometry: a flatter central zone than the cornea, surrounded by a steeper reverse curve.

mcq.q: Which wear pattern is riskiest for infection?
mcq.explanation: Overnight (extended) wear carries the highest risk of microbial keratitis of any wearing pattern.

cases.question: Give the advantages of disposable contact lenses.
cases.modelAnswer: Half a mark each: fewer deposit-related problems (papillary conjunctivitis, red eyes, reduced comfort and VA); fewer unscheduled visits; higher-water lenses for better corneal physiology; spare lenses; simpler lens care; better patient management; more patient contact.

cases.question: What are the key considerations for daily versus extended wear?
cases.modelAnswer: Half a mark each: corneal status; risk factors; Rx; tear film; lid integrity; environmental factors; individual characteristics.
